The Partial Testimony of Logs: Evaluation of Language Model Generation under Confounded Model Choice

Jikai Jin    Vasilis Syrgkanis Affiliation: {jkjin, vsyrgk}@stanford.edu
Abstract

Offline evaluation of language models from usage logs is biased when model choice is confounded: the same user-side factors that influence which model is used can also influence how its output is judged, so raw comparisons of logged scores mix self-selected populations rather than estimating a common quantity of interest. A small randomized experiment can break this bias by overriding model choice, but in practice such experiments are scarce and costly. We study a three-source design that combines a large confounded observational log (OBS) for scale, a small randomized experiment (EXP) for unconfounded scoring, and an offline simulator (SIM) that replays candidate models on cached contexts. Our main result is an identification theorem showing that the randomized experiment and the simulator are together enough to recover causal model values; the observational log enters only afterward, to reduce estimation error rather than to make the causal comparison valid. Six estimator families are evaluated in a controlled semi-synthetic validation and in two real-task cached benchmarks for summarization and coding. No family dominates every regime; relative performance depends on the amount of unbiased EXP supervision and on how closely the target reward aligns with OBS-derived structure.

1 Introduction

Offline evaluation of language models increasingly relies on deployment logs, preference data, and judge annotations collected in the wild (Zheng et al., 2024; Zhao et al., 2024; Zheng et al., 2023; Chiang et al., 2024). Once model choice is user-driven, those logs are confounded: the same unobserved factors that influence which model is used can also influence how its output is judged (Kallus et al., 2018; Rosenman et al., 2023; Cheng & Cai, 2021). Raw comparisons of logged outcomes therefore mix different self-selected subpopulations rather than a common target population. In summarization, a reader who prefers concise prose may select a model known for that style and rate it more favorably; in coding assistance, repository difficulty or developer familiarity may affect both which assistant is invoked and whether the resulting patch succeeds.

A randomized experiment breaks this link by overriding model choice. In practice, such experiments are costly and disruptive, so they remain small. Prior work studies how to combine a large confounded observational sample with a small randomized one (Kallus et al., 2018; Rosenman et al., 2023; Cheng & Cai, 2021; Lin et al., 2025; Yang et al., 2025; Colnet et al., 2024).

The problem has two parts: outcome generation and outcome scoring. Outcome generation asks which output a model would have produced on a given context; in many deployments an offline simulator (SIM) handles this by replaying models on cached contexts. Outcome scoring asks how the realized output should be evaluated without inheriting the bias in logged model choice. Separating the two yields a three-source design: a large observational log (OBS) with self-selected model choices, a small randomized experiment (EXP) with unconfounded outcome labels, and SIM outputs under alternative model choices. The goal is to estimate how each generative model would perform when logged model choice is confounded, randomized outcome labels are limited, and offline replay can regenerate candidate outputs.

Contributions. The paper makes three contributions.

  1. (C1)

    Identification (Theorem 1). Under the structural assumptions stated in Section 2, the simulator and the randomized experiment together identify causal model values. The observational log is not required for identification.

  2. (C2)

    Estimator role of OBS (post-identification only). We separate identification from estimation and compare six post-identification estimator families that differ in how they use OBS. After identification, OBS improves estimation but never serves as an identifying source. A theory-to-evidence map explains why different families help in different data regimes.

  3. (C3)

    Empirical evaluation. A controlled semi-synthetic validation and two real-task cached benchmarks (summarization, coding) compare the estimator families on held-out recommendation regret. The empirical pattern is not universal: performance depends mainly on how much unbiased experimental supervision is available, and on how well observational structure matches the reward that ultimately matters. The cached benchmarks evaluate fixed cached targets rather than the full latent population quantity one would ideally estimate.

Section 2 defines the causal graph, data sources, target estimands, and assumptions. Section 3 states and proves the SIM-plus-EXP identification result. Section 4 introduces the post-identification estimator families and the theory-to-evidence map. Section 5 describes the controlled validation and cached benchmarks; Sections 5.3.1 and 5.4 report the cached summarization and cached coding probes. Sections 6, 7, and 8 cover related work, scope and limitations, and conclusions.

2 Problem setting

OBS provides scale and auxiliary supervision from self-selected usage, EXP provides unbiased outcome labels, and SIM provides counterfactual outputs. Theorem 1 shows that EXP and SIM identify the target, while OBS only improves statistical efficiency afterward. Figures 1 and 2 illustrate the causal structure and the division of labor.

2.1 Variables and causal structure

We study a five-variable graph (X,U,A,M,Y)(X,U,A,M,Y) shown in Figure 1, where XX is the observed context, U∈ℝduU\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{u}} is an unobserved user state, A∈𝒜A\in\mathcal{A} indexes the chosen generative model, MM is the generated output, and Y∈[0,1]Y\in[0,1] is the scalar outcome. Confounding arises because the latent state UU affects both model choice and outcome. Beyond ordinary confounding, the graph imposes two structural restrictions: conditional on (X,A)(X,A), the latent user state UU does not directly affect the mediator MM, and AA affects the outcome YY only through MM. These assumptions are natural in stateless generative systems, where the model’s behavior is determined by its input and internal randomness rather than by who is asking.

2.2 Accessible data sources

Three data sources are available, each contributing something the others cannot provide alone.

Observational log (OBS).

OBS is a large observational dataset DOBS={(Xi,Ai,Mi,Yi,Zi)}i=1nOBS,D_{\mathrm{OBS}}=\{(X_{i},A_{i},M_{i},Y_{i},Z_{i})\}_{i=1}^{n_{\mathrm{OBS}}}, where AiA_{i} may depend on the corresponding latent state UiU_{i} and Zi∈[0,1]KZ_{i}\in[0,1]^{K} are KK auxiliary labels that may or may not be available. The auxiliary labels ZiZ_{i} provide extra supervision for learning a compact proxy representation of the context–output pair; user feedback ratings and pairwise preferences are natural sources and can often be collected at scale (Christiano et al., 2017; Ouyang et al., 2022; Chiang et al., 2024).

Randomized experiment (EXP).

EXP is a much smaller dataset DEXP={(Xj,Aj,Mj,Yj)}j=1nEXP,D_{\mathrm{EXP}}=\{(X_{j},A_{j},M_{j},Y_{j})\}_{j=1}^{n_{\mathrm{EXP}}}, in which model choice is randomized and therefore unconfounded. Since AjA_{j} is drawn from the experimental action set 𝒜EXP\mathcal{A}_{\mathrm{EXP}} according to a fixed distribution, A⟂UA\perp U and A⟂U|XA\perp U\mid X, so EXP outcomes are causally interpretable. Randomizing model choice disrupts user experience, which is why these experiments remain small in practice.

Offline simulator (SIM).

The simulator reruns any generative model on any context and returns a mediator draw from M∼psim(⋅∣X=x,A=a).M\sim p_{\mathrm{sim}}(\cdot\mid X=x,A=a). Operationally, SIM reruns generative model aa on held-out context xx and records the generated output. In generative systems, SIM is especially natural because prompts, retrieved documents, tool traces, and other environment inputs can often be stored as deterministic inputs, while the remaining randomness comes from the generative model itself.

2.3 Target estimands

Two practical targets matter.

Marginal model value.

How well would each model perform on average if used by the full target population? The marginal model value is the main target for offline comparison of a fixed set of generative models, and it corresponds to the target estimand

μ⁡(a):=𝔼⁡[Y⁡(do⁡(A=a))].\mu(a):=\mathbb{E}\!\left[Y\big(\mathrm{do}(A=a)\big)\right].
Context-conditional model value.

Given a particular observed context xx, what outcome would each model deliver on average? The context-conditional value is the key target for recommendation and personalization, and it corresponds to the context-level function

q⁡(x,a):=𝔼⁡[Y⁡(do⁡(A=a))∣X=x].q(x,a):=\mathbb{E}\!\left[Y\big(\mathrm{do}(A=a)\big)\mid X=x\right].

Section 3 shows how both targets are recovered: SIM supplies the model-specific mediator distribution and EXP provides unconfounded scores for realized outputs.

In real cached benchmarks, we instead evaluate the finite cached target

qcache​(x,a):=r⋆​(x,mcache​(x,a)),q_{\mathrm{cache}}(x,a):=r^{\star}\!\bigl(x,m_{\mathrm{cache}}(x,a)\bigr),

where mcache​(x,a)m_{\mathrm{cache}}(x,a) is the stored output for that context–model pair. The finite cached target approximates q⁡(x,a)q(x,a); the superpopulation estimand remains latent.

2.4 Design assumptions for SIM-based identification

Assumption A1 (Randomization in EXP).

In EXP, AA is randomized over 𝒜EXP\mathcal{A}_{\mathrm{EXP}} so that A⟂UA\perp U and A⟂U|XA\perp U\mid X hold.

Randomization is the sole source of unconfounded outcome information; without it, identification is impossible regardless of OBS size.

Assumption A2 (SIM validity and support).

The simulator matches the interventional mediator distribution, psim​(m∣x,a)=ℙ⁡(M=m∣X=x,do⁡(A=a))p_{\mathrm{sim}}(m\mid x,a)=\mathbb{P}(M=m\mid X=x,\mathrm{do}(A=a)), and is supported within the EXP mediator support: for every xx in the EXP context support and every a∈𝒜EXPa\in\mathcal{A}_{\mathrm{EXP}},

supppsim(⋅∣x,a)⊆suppℙ(M∣X=x,A=a,EXP).\operatorname{supp}p_{\mathrm{sim}}(\cdot\mid x,a)\;\subseteq\;\operatorname{supp}\mathbb{P}(M\mid X=x,A=a,\mathrm{EXP}).

Throughout the paper, “the shared EXP/SIM support” refers to this support condition. SIM validity is satisfied whenever any randomness in the generated output comes from the generative model itself and all deployment-time inputs that affect the generative model’s behavior are included in XX.

Assumption A3 (Outcome consistency under intervention).

OBS and EXP measure the same outcome YY, and the conditional outcome law given (X,M,U)(X,M,U) is invariant across OBS, EXP, and the post-intervention world: for every (x,m,u)(x,m,u) on the relevant support,

ℙ⁡(Y∣X=x,M=m,U=u,OBS)\displaystyle\mathbb{P}(Y\mid X=x,M=m,U=u,\mathrm{OBS})\; =ℙ⁡(Y∣X=x,M=m,U=u,EXP)\displaystyle=\;\mathbb{P}(Y\mid X=x,M=m,U=u,\mathrm{EXP})
=ℙ⁡(Y∣X=x,M=m,U=u,do⁡(A=a)).\displaystyle=\;\mathbb{P}(Y\mid X=x,M=m,U=u,\mathrm{do}(A=a)).

Only the model-choice mechanism differs across OBS, EXP, and intervention. Without this, EXP supervision could not transport either to the intervention or to the OBS-trained reward models.

Assumption A4 (No latent mediator confounding; single-round generation).

Conditional on (X,A)(X,A), the latent state UU is independent of the mediator MM in both OBS and EXP, and under do⁡(A=a)\mathrm{do}(A=a):

U⟂M|X,A.U\perp M\mid X,A.

Equivalently, the SCM has no edge U→MU\to M once (X,A)(X,A) is fixed, and any deployment-time inputs that drive the generative model are absorbed into XX. The same structural restriction appears in Figure 1; promoting it to a formal assumption combines with A1’s randomization in the mediator step of the proof of Theorem 1. A4 restricts the framework to single-round, stateless generation. In repeated, adaptive, or multi-round interactions the residual dependence of MM on UU given (X,A)(X,A) is generally nonzero, so A4 fails.

Assumption A5 (Context distribution alignment).

The marginal model value μ⁡(a)\mu(a) is defined with respect to a target context distribution PXtgtP_{X}^{\mathrm{tgt}} that coincides with the EXP context distribution: PXtgt=PXEXPP_{X}^{\mathrm{tgt}}=P_{X}^{\mathrm{EXP}}. Equivalently, the EXP sample is drawn from the same context population over which μ⁡(a)\mu(a) is averaged. When this fails, only q⁡(x,a)q(x,a) on the shared support is identified, and any reweighting to a different PXtgtP_{X}^{\mathrm{tgt}} requires standard transportability and trial-generalizability arguments (Cole & Stuart, 2010; Pearl & Bareinboim, 2011; Bareinboim & Pearl, 2016) that are outside the scope of this paper.

3 Identification

The remaining identification problem is to score generated outputs without bias. EXP provides that scoring rule, while SIM provides the interventional mediator distribution. Throughout, we evaluate only actions in the experimental action set 𝒜EXP\mathcal{A}_{\mathrm{EXP}} and mediator values on the shared support of the EXP law of M∣X=x,A=aM\mid X=x,A=a and the corresponding SIM law psim(⋅∣x,a)p_{\mathrm{sim}}(\cdot\mid x,a). Define r⋆(x,m):=𝔼[Y∣X=x,M=m,EXP]r^{\star}(x,m):=\mathbb{E}[Y\mid X=x,M=m,\mathrm{EXP}].

Theorem 1 (SIM plus EXP identifies causal value).

Under the causal graph in Figure 1 and Assumptions A1–A5, for every xx in the EXP context support and every a∈𝒜EXPa\in\mathcal{A}_{\mathrm{EXP}},

q(x,a)=𝔼[Y(do(A=a))∣X=x]=𝔼M∼psim(⋅∣x,a)[r⋆(x,M)],q(x,a)=\mathbb{E}\!\left[Y\big(\mathrm{do}(A=a)\big)\mid X=x\right]=\mathbb{E}_{M\sim p_{\mathrm{sim}}(\cdot\mid x,a)}\!\left[r^{\star}(x,M)\right], (1)

and therefore, with μ⁡(a)\mu(a) defined under the target context distribution PXtgt=PXEXPP_{X}^{\mathrm{tgt}}=P_{X}^{\mathrm{EXP}} of Assumption A5,

μ(a)=𝔼X∼PXtgt[q(X,a)]=𝔼X∼PXtgt[𝔼M∼psim(⋅∣X,a)[r⋆(X,M)]].\mu(a)=\mathbb{E}_{X\sim P_{X}^{\mathrm{tgt}}}[q(X,a)]=\mathbb{E}_{X\sim P_{X}^{\mathrm{tgt}}}\!\left[\mathbb{E}_{M\sim p_{\mathrm{sim}}(\cdot\mid X,a)}\!\left[r^{\star}(X,M)\right]\right]. (2)

Hence both q⁡(x,a)q(x,a) and μ⁡(a)\mu(a) are identified from EXP and SIM on the shared EXP/SIM support. In particular, OBS need not satisfy any unconfoundedness condition for identification.

Proof sketch.

The proof uses the assumptions one at a time in four steps.

  1. Step 1.

    Combine A1 and A4 to obtain conditional independence. Assumption A1 gives A⟂U|XA\perp U\mid X in EXP, and Assumption A4 gives U⟂M|X,AU\perp M\mid X,A in EXP and under intervention. The chain rule yields U⟂(A,M)|XU\perp(A,M)\mid X in EXP, so the EXP conditional regression r⋆(x,m)=𝔼[Y∣X=x,M=m,EXP]r^{\star}(x,m)=\mathbb{E}[Y\mid X=x,M=m,\mathrm{EXP}] is unbiased for the causal scoring rule on the shared EXP/SIM support.

  2. Step 2.

    Use A3 to transport scoring across OBS, EXP, and intervention. Assumption A3 states that the conditional outcome law given (X,M,U)(X,M,U) is the same in OBS, in EXP, and under do⁡(A=a)\mathrm{do}(A=a). Combined with Step 1, this means r⋆​(x,m)r^{\star}(x,m) is also the conditional outcome regression under do⁡(A=a)\mathrm{do}(A=a) on the shared support.

  3. Step 3.

    Use A2 to plug in the SIM mediator distribution. Assumption A2 states that psim​(m∣x,a)p_{\mathrm{sim}}(m\mid x,a) is the interventional mediator distribution. Marginalizing r⋆r^{\star} over MM under psim(⋅∣x,a)p_{\mathrm{sim}}(\cdot\mid x,a) therefore identifies q⁡(x,a)q(x,a), giving (1).

  4. Step 4.

    Use A5 to identify the marginal model value. Assumption A5 fixes the target context distribution to PXtgt=PXEXPP_{X}^{\mathrm{tgt}}=P_{X}^{\mathrm{EXP}}, so averaging q⁡(X,a)q(X,a) under that distribution identifies μ⁡(a)\mu(a), giving (2).

The full proof is in Appendix C.1. Identification requires both SIM, to regenerate outputs, and EXP, to provide outcome labels for those outputs. Conditioning on (X,M)(X,M) in OBS does not block confounding through UU when Assumption A4 fails or OBS routes AA on UU. Appendix A.1 gives the explicit derivations.

From identification to the experimental design.

The controlled semi-synthetic validation and the real cached benchmarks probe different parts of the theorem. The controlled semi-synthetic validation (Section 5.2) directly probes the theorem-level target: a known latent reward generator varies only β\beta, nOBSn_{\mathrm{OBS}}, and nEXPn_{\mathrm{EXP}}, so estimator gaps reflect SIM-plus-EXP identification followed by post-identification estimation. The real cached benchmarks (Sections 5.3.1 and 5.4) report recommendation regret against the finite cached target qcacheq_{\mathrm{cache}}, with one cached output per context-action pair and synthetic OBS/EXP resampling. They diagnose the post-identification estimator families within those benchmark constructions rather than testing Theorem 1 directly. In all settings, the estimator design in Section 4 uses OBS only after identification to reduce variance or improve approximation.

4 Estimators

After SIM and EXP identify the target, the remaining question is how OBS can reduce estimation error. The six estimator families differ only in how they use OBS after identification: some ignore OBS outcomes entirely, some use OBS only to learn a lower-dimensional proxy representation, and some use OBS outcomes directly through a baseline or pooled fit. Exact objectives, proxy-learning details, and value-aggregation formulas are deferred to Appendix A.2 and Appendix A.4.

Throughout, z=(x,m)z=(x,m) denotes a context–mediator pair, and all reward models start from text features φ⁡(z)\varphi(z). Hybrid methods use OBS auxiliary labels only to learn a lower-dimensional proxy representation ψ⁡(z)\psi(z), in the same spirit as text embeddings adapted for causal adjustment (Veitch et al., 2020). The proxy only makes the EXP-side fit lower-dimensional and leaves the identified target unchanged.

The estimator comparison is guided by three evidence tiers. The identification theorem is part of the main paper. The estimator-comparison results in Appendix C provide formal support for several oracle and approximation statements. Target-alignment patterns in the benchmarks diagnose whether a target reward aligns with a proxy, baseline, or correction class. They provide empirical rather than formal evidence. Table 2 summarizes this map.

4.1 Reward-model estimators

All six reward models minimize penalized squared loss with predictions clipped to [0,1][0,1]. They differ only in whether and how they use OBS. Table 1 summarizes the six families; Appendix A.2 gives exact objectives and benchmark-specific instantiations.

Prediction-form summary.

Each family produces a clipped predicted reward r^​(x,m)\widehat{r}(x,m) from one of the following forms; here φ⁡(z)\varphi(z) is the raw text feature, ψ⁡(z)\psi(z) is the OBS-derived proxy representation, fOBS​(z)f_{\mathrm{OBS}}(z) is the OBS-trained predictor (so r^OBS​(z)=fOBS​(z)\widehat{r}_{\mathrm{OBS}}(z)=f_{\mathrm{OBS}}(z) for O​B​S−O​n​l​y{\color[rgb]{0.1094,0.1953,0.3203}OBS-Only}{}), and αcorr∈[0,1]\alpha_{\mathrm{corr}}\in[0,1], λ∈[0,1]\lambda\in[0,1] are EXP-side tuning weights chosen by causal cross-validation:

r^EXP​(z)\displaystyle\widehat{r}_{\mathrm{EXP}}(z) =clip[0,1]​(w^EXP⊤​φ​(z)+b^EXP),\displaystyle=\mathrm{clip}_{[0,1]}\!\bigl(\widehat{w}_{\mathrm{EXP}}^{\top}\varphi(z)+\widehat{b}_{\mathrm{EXP}}\bigr),
r^ψ​(z)\displaystyle\widehat{r}_{\psi}(z) =clip[0,1]​(w^ψ⊤​ψ​(z)+b^ψ),\displaystyle=\mathrm{clip}_{[0,1]}\!\bigl(\widehat{w}_{\psi}^{\top}\psi(z)+\widehat{b}_{\psi}\bigr),
r^G​(z)\displaystyle\widehat{r}_{\mathrm{G}}(z) =clip[0,1]​(fOBS​(z)−αcorr​(θ^B⊤​B​(ψ⁡(z))+c^B)),\displaystyle=\mathrm{clip}_{[0,1]}\!\Bigl(f_{\mathrm{OBS}}(z)-\alpha_{\mathrm{corr}}\bigl(\widehat{\theta}_{B}^{\top}B(\psi(z))+\widehat{c}_{B}\bigr)\Bigr),
r^C​(z)\displaystyle\widehat{r}_{\mathrm{C}}(z) =clip[0,1]​(w^λ⊤​φ​(z)+b^λ),\displaystyle=\mathrm{clip}_{[0,1]}\!\bigl(\widehat{w}_{\lambda}^{\top}\varphi(z)+\widehat{b}_{\lambda}\bigr),
r^CR​(z)\displaystyle\widehat{r}_{\mathrm{CR}}(z) =clip[0,1]​(fOBS​(z)+g^res​(z)).\displaystyle=\mathrm{clip}_{[0,1]}\!\bigl(f_{\mathrm{OBS}}(z)+\widehat{g}_{\mathrm{res}}(z)\bigr).

In words: r^EXP\widehat{r}_{\mathrm{EXP}} regresses YY on φ\varphi using EXP; r^ψ\widehat{r}_{\psi} regresses YY on the OBS-derived proxy ψ\psi using EXP; and r^G\widehat{r}_{\mathrm{G}} adds an EXP-fit correction to the OBS baseline fOBSf_{\mathrm{OBS}} in proxy space. r^C\widehat{r}_{\mathrm{C}} pools the OBS and EXP regression problems on φ\varphi with mixing weight λ\lambda (λ=1\lambda=1 gives O​B​S−O​n​l​y{\color[rgb]{0.1094,0.1953,0.3203}OBS-Only}{}, λ=0\lambda=0 gives E​X​P−O​n​l​y{\color[rgb]{0.3594,0.1016,0.1641}EXP-Only}{}), and r^CR\widehat{r}_{\mathrm{CR}} adds an EXP residual fit g^res\widehat{g}_{\mathrm{res}} in proxy space to fOBSf_{\mathrm{OBS}} on the residual target Y−fOBS​(z)Y-f_{\mathrm{OBS}}(z). Appendix A.2 gives the exact objectives and the tuning rule for αcorr\alpha_{\mathrm{corr}}, λ\lambda, and the basis BB.

From reward models to model values.

Given a fitted reward r^\widehat{r}, the direct method (DM) and doubly robust (DR) value estimators (Robins et al., 1994; Bang & Robins, 2005; Dudík et al., 2011; Dudík et al., 2014; Jiang & Li, 2016) plug r^\widehat{r} into the identification formula (1)–(2). For each held-out context xx and action aa, the cached benchmarks compute

q^DM​(x,a)=r^​(x,mcache​(x,a)),\widehat{q}^{\mathrm{DM}}(x,a)=\widehat{r}(x,m_{\mathrm{cache}}(x,a)),

i.e. the fitted reward at the cached mediator; the controlled semi-synthetic validation, which has access to a real SIM, instead averages r^\widehat{r} over a SIM mediator sample. The marginal value is μ^DM​(a)=𝔼X∼PXEXP​[q^DM​(X,a)]\widehat{\mu}^{\mathrm{DM}}(a)=\mathbb{E}_{X\sim P_{X}^{\mathrm{EXP}}}[\widehat{q}^{\mathrm{DM}}(X,a)], with the expectation replaced by an empirical average over the held-out EXP context split.

The doubly robust estimator (DR) corrects μ^DM​(a)\widehat{\mu}^{\mathrm{DM}}(a) on EXP. With KK-fold cross-fitting and uniform EXP randomization pEXP​(a)=1/|𝒜EXP|p_{\mathrm{EXP}}(a)=1/|\mathcal{A}_{\mathrm{EXP}}|, write r^(−k)\widehat{r}^{(-k)} for the reward model trained on EXP folds {1,…,K}∖{k}\{1,\ldots,K\}\setminus\{k\} and let k⁡(j)k(j) be the fold containing EXP point jj. The DR estimator for the marginal model value is

μ^DR​(a)=μ^DM​(a)+1nEXP​∑j=1nEXP𝕀{Aj=a}pEXP​(a)​ε^j​(a),\widehat{\mu}^{\mathrm{DR}}(a)\;=\;\widehat{\mu}^{\mathrm{DM}}(a)\;+\;\frac{1}{n_{\mathrm{EXP}}}\sum_{j=1}^{n_{\mathrm{EXP}}}\frac{\mathbb{I}\{A_{j}=a\}}{p_{\mathrm{EXP}}(a)}\,\widehat{\varepsilon}_{j}(a), (3)

where ε^j​(a):=Yj−r^(−k⁡(j))​(Xj,Mj)\widehat{\varepsilon}_{j}(a):=Y_{j}-\widehat{r}^{(-k(j))}(X_{j},M_{j}) is the cross-fitted EXP residual. Both terms in (3) target the marginal value μ⁡(a)\mu(a) under Assumption A5. The complete DM/DR formulas and cross-fitting protocol are given in Appendix A.4.

  1. 1.

    Use only EXP. EXP-Only is the unbiased baseline: it fits a clipped ridge reward model using only randomized EXP outcomes (the standard randomized-trial regression baseline used as a reference point in hybrid OBS–EXP work, e.g. Kallus et al., 2018; Rosenman et al., 2023; Yang et al., 2025), and pays for that with high variance when EXP is small.

  2. 2.

    Use OBS only to learn a representation. Representation-EXP still relies on EXP for causal supervision, but it first uses OBS auxiliary labels to learn ψ⁡(z)\psi(z) and then fits the reward head on that representation (Veitch et al., 2020). It helps when the target varies mainly along directions preserved by ψ\psi, and it hurts when ψ\psi discards directions that matter for the target.

  3. 3.

    Use OBS outcomes, calibrated by EXP. These methods use OBS for signal and EXP for calibration. O​B​S−O​n​l​y{\color[rgb]{0.1094,0.1953,0.3203}OBS-Only}{} is the uncalibrated endpoint — a clipped ridge regression on OBS outcomes alone, the canonical biased-but-low-variance baseline in the OBS–EXP combination literature (Kallus et al., 2018; Rosenman et al., 2023; Cheng & Cai, 2021; Lin et al., 2025; Yang et al., 2025) — and the next three methods differ only in how they calibrate it.

3.1 Grounded Correction (Grounded). Inspired by experimental grounding (Kallus et al., 2018), Grounded starts from the OBS predictor fOBSf_{\mathrm{OBS}} and uses EXP to learn a correction in proxy space. In the benchmark implementation, that correction is chosen from a small basis library rather than from a single linear head. Its final prediction is

rground,B,αcorr​(z)=clip[0,1]​(fOBS​(z)−αcorr​(θ^B⊤​B​(ψ~​(z))+c^B)),r_{\mathrm{ground},B,\alpha_{\mathrm{corr}}}(z)\;=\;\mathrm{clip}_{[0,1]}\!\Big(f_{\mathrm{OBS}}(z)-\alpha_{\mathrm{corr}}\big(\widehat{\theta}_{B}^{\top}B(\tilde{\psi}(z))+\widehat{c}_{B}\big)\Big),

where ψ~​(z)\tilde{\psi}(z) is the low-dimensional proxy representation and BB is selected from a small fixed basis library on that proxy space. The method is most attractive when OBS already captures the coarse reward surface and EXP mainly needs to remove a lower-dimensional bias. Appendix A.2 gives the exact fitting and tuning details.

3.2 Cross-validated Causal Inference (CVCI). CVCI (Yang et al., 2025), building on the broader OBS–EXP combination literature (Rosenman et al., 2023; Cheng & Cai, 2021; Lin et al., 2025), pools the OBS and EXP regression problems directly and chooses the pooling weight λ∈[0,1]\lambda\in[0,1] by causal cross-validation on EXP. Concretely, the pooled coefficient solves

(w^λ,b^λ)=arg⁡minw,b​{(1−λ)​ℒEXP​(w,b,φ,Y)+λ​ℒOBS​(w,b,φ,Y)+α​‖w‖22},(\widehat{w}_{\lambda},\widehat{b}_{\lambda})=\arg\min_{w,b}\Bigl\{(1-\lambda)\,\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{EXP}}(w,b;\varphi,Y)+\lambda\,\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{OBS}}(w,b;\varphi,Y)+\alpha\|w\|_{2}^{2}\Bigr\}, (4)

where ℒ𝒟​(w,b,ϕ,Y):=∑i∈𝒟(Yi−(w⊤​ϕ​(zi)+b))2\mathcal{L}_{\mathcal{D}}(w,b;\phi,Y):=\sum_{i\in\mathcal{D}}(Y_{i}-(w^{\top}\phi(z_{i})+b))^{2} is the squared-error loss on dataset 𝒟\mathcal{D} in feature map ϕ\phi, so λ=1\lambda=1 recovers the O​B​S−O​n​l​y{\color[rgb]{0.1094,0.1953,0.3203}OBS-Only}{} regression and λ=0\lambda=0 recovers the E​X​P−O​n​l​y{\color[rgb]{0.3594,0.1016,0.1641}EXP-Only}{} regression on φ\varphi. The pooling weight λ\lambda is selected by minimizing held-out causal-CV loss on EXP at the model level (Appendix A.8), anchoring the bias–variance interpolation to randomized outcomes.

3.3 CVCI-Residual. CVCI-Residual extends the CVCI pooling rule of Yang et al. (2025) by first residualizing around the OBS baseline (replacing the regression target YY with Y−fOBS​(z)Y-f_{\mathrm{OBS}}(z)) and then running a λ\lambda-pooled fit in the proxy space ψ⁡(z)\psi(z):

(w^λres,b^λres)=arg⁡minw,b​{(1−λ)​ℒEXP​(w,b,ψ,Y−fOBS)+λ​ℒOBS​(w,b,ψ,Y−fOBS)+α​‖w‖22},(\widehat{w}^{\mathrm{res}}_{\lambda},\widehat{b}^{\mathrm{res}}_{\lambda})=\arg\min_{w,b}\Bigl\{(1-\lambda)\,\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{EXP}}(w,b;\psi,Y-f_{\mathrm{OBS}})+\lambda\,\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{OBS}}(w,b;\psi,Y-f_{\mathrm{OBS}})+\alpha\|w\|_{2}^{2}\Bigr\}, (5)

yielding g^res​(z)=(w^λres)⊤​ψ​(z)+b^λres\widehat{g}_{\mathrm{res}}(z)=(\widehat{w}^{\mathrm{res}}_{\lambda})^{\top}\psi(z)+\widehat{b}^{\mathrm{res}}_{\lambda} and the final prediction clip[0,1]​(fOBS​(z)+g^res​(z))\mathrm{clip}_{[0,1]}\!\big(f_{\mathrm{OBS}}(z)+\widehat{g}_{\mathrm{res}}(z)\big). It targets settings where OBS already captures the hard part of the reward surface and EXP is mainly needed to calibrate a simpler discrepancy. When residual-CVCI hyperparameter CV scores tie within numerical tolerance, the tie is broken toward the more regularized candidate; Appendix A.2 and Appendix A.8 give the full tuning protocol and additional implementation details.

Family-level interpretation.

The six items above are estimator families with benchmark-specific instantiations. The proxy channel, the OBS baseline, the basis library, the pooling rule, and the EXP-side tuning protocol differ across benchmarks (see Table 8 in Appendix A.2). The empirical comparisons in Sections 5–5.4 diagnose those family-level instantiations.

5 Empirical benchmarks

5.1 Benchmark setup

Across all empirical benchmarks, the task is the same: estimate a reward surface, recommend the best action on each held-out context, and measure held-out recommendation regret. Two quantities recur throughout the benchmarks: β\beta controls the OBS choice law, and the real cached benchmarks replace the latent target qq with the finite cached target qcacheq_{\mathrm{cache}}. Each benchmark setting specifies a training-context distribution, a held-out test set, an action set, a simulator, an experimental reward map, and an observational logging family. Within one such cell, the observational law factors as

pOBS​(x,u,a,m,y)=Ptr​(x)​P​(u∣x)​pOBSβ​(a∣x,u)​psim​(m∣x,a)​PY​(y∣x,m,u),p_{\mathrm{OBS}}(x,u,a,m,y)=P_{\mathrm{tr}}(x)\,P(u\mid x)\,p_{\mathrm{OBS}}^{\beta}(a\mid x,u)\,p_{\mathrm{sim}}(m\mid x,a)\,P_{Y}(y\mid x,m,u),

and the experimental law replaces the choice model by an unconfounded randomization rule πEXP​(a∣x)\pi_{\mathrm{EXP}}(a\mid x):

pEXP​(x,u,a,m,y)=Ptr​(x)​P​(u∣x)​πEXP​(a∣x)​psim​(m∣x,a)​PY​(y∣x,m,u).p_{\mathrm{EXP}}(x,u,a,m,y)=P_{\mathrm{tr}}(x)\,P(u\mid x)\,\pi_{\mathrm{EXP}}(a\mid x)\,p_{\mathrm{sim}}(m\mid x,a)\,P_{Y}(y\mid x,m,u).

Here PYP_{Y} is the benchmark-specific outcome law. In the main-text benchmark settings, πEXP​(a∣x)=1/|𝒜|\pi_{\mathrm{EXP}}(a\mid x)=1/|\mathcal{A}|, and r⋆(x,m)=𝔼[Y∣X=x,M=m,EXP]r^{\star}(x,m)=\mathbb{E}[Y\mid X=x,M=m,\mathrm{EXP}] integrates out U|X=xU\mid X=x under pEXPp_{\mathrm{EXP}}. The identified target remains

q(x,a)=𝔼M∼psim(⋅∣x,a)[r⋆(x,M)].q(x,a)=\mathbb{E}_{M\sim p_{\mathrm{sim}}(\cdot\mid x,a)}[r^{\star}(x,M)].

Each estimator returns q^\widehat{q}, inducing the recommendation rule π^​(x)=arg⁡maxa∈𝒜​q^​(x,a)\widehat{\pi}(x)=\arg\max_{a\in\mathcal{A}}\widehat{q}(x,a). We evaluate that rule by held-out recommendation regret,

Regrettest=1|𝒳test|​∑x∈𝒳test[maxa∈𝒜⁡q⁡(x,a)−q⁡(x,π^​(x))].\mathrm{Regret}_{\mathrm{test}}=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{X}_{\mathrm{test}}|}\sum_{x\in\mathcal{X}_{\mathrm{test}}}\Big[\max_{a\in\mathcal{A}}q(x,a)-q(x,\widehat{\pi}(x))\Big].

The β\beta-indexed observational choice law is benchmark-specific. In the appendix controlled validation, pOBSβ​(a∣x,u)=(1−β)​πX​(a∣x)+β​πU​(a∣u)p_{\mathrm{OBS}}^{\beta}(a\mid x,u)=(1-\beta)\pi_{X}(a\mid x)+\beta\,\pi_{U}(a\mid u), where πX\pi_{X} is a context-driven policy and πU\pi_{U} is a latent-user policy. Thus β=0\beta=0 removes latent-user routing, whereas β=1\beta=1 uses only the latent-user component. Section 5.3.1 instead uses a softmax router in which β\beta scales the latent-user logit contribution.

The real cached benchmarks fix one realized mediator mcache​(x,a)m_{\mathrm{cache}}(x,a) for each context-action pair and report the finite cached target qcache​(x,a)=r⋆​(x,mcache​(x,a))q_{\mathrm{cache}}(x,a)=r^{\star}\!\bigl(x,m_{\mathrm{cache}}(x,a)\bigr). Their reported recommendation regret therefore replaces qq by qcacheq_{\mathrm{cache}} on the held-out cache. Randomness then comes from OBS/EXP sampling and the benchmark’s latent draws, not from regenerating mediators at evaluation time.

5.2 Controlled validation as a theory bridge

The controlled semi-synthetic validation uses the summarization task family but replaces judged rewards by a known latent reward generator. The validation keeps the SIM/EXP/OBS structure fixed while varying confounding strength β\beta, the observational budget nOBSn_{\mathrm{OBS}}, and the randomized budget nEXPn_{\mathrm{EXP}}. The validation connects the estimator theory to observable behavior. When EXP is scarce, OBS-assisted estimators can improve held-out recommendation performance. With a larger randomized sample, EXP-only and directly pooled estimators become competitive. No single estimator dominates every regime. The full generator, protocol, and 2424-cell winner map are in Appendix A.9 and Appendix A.10.

This controlled validation isolates how data budget and confounding strength change performance when the true interventional surface is known. The real summarization and coding benchmarks below then test the same estimator families on finite cached targets qcacheq_{\mathrm{cache}}, where reward definition and auxiliary-feature alignment become the main explanatory variables.

5.3 Main-text benchmarks

The main paper reports the controlled validation and two real-task cached benchmarks with synthetic OBS/EXP resampling. The first cached benchmark is summarization on CNN/DailyMail11 1 https://huggingface.co/datasets/ccdv/cnn_dailymail (Hermann et al., 2015; Nallapati et al., 2016; See et al., 2017). The second is coding on SWE-bench Verified22 2 https://huggingface.co/datasets/princeton-nlp/SWE-bench_Verified, a human-validated 500-instance subset of SWE-bench (Jimenez et al., 2024; OpenAI, 2024), with candidate patches drawn from the BouncerBench public patch pool33 3 https://github.com/uw-swag/BouncerBench/releases/download/paper/all_patches.csv (Mathews & Nagappan, 2025). Both benchmarks use real tasks, real candidate model outputs, and real LLM-judged or program-test rewards on those outputs. Their OBS and EXP mechanisms are benchmark constructions obtained by resampling and reweighting the same cached pool under specified choice and randomization rules. Table 3 lists the source data, cached objects, and targets. All benchmarks use family-level instantiations of the estimators in Section 4, and the reported results diagnose those families within the benchmark constructions.

5.3.1 Real-task cached summarization benchmark with synthetic OBS/EXP resampling

The cached summarization benchmark uses CNN/DailyMail articles and LLM-judged rubric scores. Its OBS and EXP samples are constructed by resampling and reweighting the same cached pool under specified routing and randomization rules. The summarization benchmark fixes one judged cached summary for each article–model pair and evaluates two reward maps on that same cache (Table 3). 5.3.2 Summarization: supervision scarcity and reward shape

In the cached summarization benchmark, C​V​C​I{\color[rgb]{0.3207,0.098,0.1488}CVCI}{} has the best average rank, top-3 coverage, and excess regret across 30 seeds and 48 settings (Table 4). The gap to the next family (about 0.04 in excess regret to O​B​S−O​n​l​y{\color[rgb]{0.1094,0.1953,0.3203}OBS-Only}{}) is small relative to the spread of cell-level standard errors reported in Appendix A.6, so this result reads as family-level evidence within this benchmark instantiation. The remaining tables explain that pattern. Table 5 shows that increasing nEXPn_{\mathrm{EXP}} lowers regret for the EXP-based estimators much more than increasing nOBSn_{\mathrm{OBS}} under the smooth reward. That pattern matches the estimator view in Table 2: once EXP and SIM identify the target, additional randomized labels can improve EXP-side reward fits. Table 6 then changes the target reward while holding the cached outputs fixed. The regret increase and the drop in rubric-linear fit serve as an empirical diagnostic of target alignment rather than a formal oracle statement.

In Table 6, the two held-out R2R^{2} values are out-of-sample linear fits of the cached target surface using the auxiliary proxy representation and the raw rubric vector s⁡(x,a)s(x,a), respectively. Table 7 reports model-level value RMSE for DM and DR. In this benchmark, DR mainly helps OBS-heavy methods; DM remains stronger for the other families. Appendix A.6 gives the budget-specific breakdown and implementation details.

Benchmark-instantiation reading.

In this cached summarization benchmark, the raw judged dimensions already give a high held-out R2R^{2} for the target reward (Table 6). Table 5 shows two patterns: C​V​C​I{\color[rgb]{0.3207,0.098,0.1488}CVCI}{} already attains the lowest regret at nEXP=20n_{\mathrm{EXP}}=20 and stays near that level as nEXPn_{\mathrm{EXP}} grows, while E​X​P−O​n​l​y{\color[rgb]{0.3594,0.1016,0.1641}EXP-Only}{} and R​e​p​r​e​s​e​n​t​a​t​i​o​n−E​X​P{\color[rgb]{0.1719,0.2891,0.1172}Representation-EXP}{} improve substantially with more EXP labels and approach the C​V​C​I{\color[rgb]{0.3207,0.098,0.1488}CVCI}{} floor at nEXP=200n_{\mathrm{EXP}}=200. Additional EXP labels mainly help the EXP-anchored families catch up to the OBS-pooled C​V​C​I{\color[rgb]{0.3207,0.098,0.1488}CVCI}{} floor rather than lower that floor.

5.4 Real-task cached coding benchmark with synthetic OBS/EXP resampling

The cached coding benchmark uses SWE-bench Verified issues (Jimenez et al., 2024; OpenAI, 2024) and one cached candidate patch for each issue–agent pair (Table 3). Candidate patches come from BouncerBench (Mathews & Nagappan, 2025), and the agent baselines follow the SWE-agent setup (Yang et al., 2024). The cached patches and program-test outcomes are real, and the OBS and EXP mechanisms are benchmark constructions over the cached pool. Evaluation averages over a fixed set of benchmark user types and reports regret on the finite cached target qcacheq_{\mathrm{cache}}.

Each cached patch is scored by four components c1,c2,c3,c4c_{1},c_{2},c_{3},c_{4}, where c1c_{1} records true fix success and c2,c3,c4c_{2},c_{3},c_{4} summarize patch size, locality, and issue focus. These patch-quality components can disagree with true fix success, which is why changing the reward definition matters here.

Method rankings change as the reward shifts weight from patch quality to true fix success. The shift is controlled by αfix\alpha_{\mathrm{fix}}, which weights true fix success, and by ωweak\omega_{\mathrm{weak}}, which determines whether the non-success components are aggregated additively or by a weakest-link rule. The first, αfix\alpha_{\mathrm{fix}}, controls how much weight the reward places on true fix success. The second, ωweak\omega_{\mathrm{weak}}, controls whether the non-success components are aggregated additively or through a weakest-link rule.

For user type uu with weights wu=(wu​1,wu​2,wu​3,wu​4)w_{u}=(w_{u1},w_{u2},w_{u3},w_{u4}), normalized non-success weights are w¯u​k=wu​k/(wu​2+wu​3+wu​4)\bar{w}_{uk}=w_{uk}/(w_{u2}+w_{u3}+w_{u4}) for k∈{2,3,4}k\in\{2,3,4\}, and gu​(c2,c3,c4)=(1−ωweak)​∑k=24w¯u​k​ck+ωweak​min⁡{c2,c3,c4}g_{u}(c_{2},c_{3},c_{4})=(1-\omega_{\mathrm{weak}})\sum_{k=2}^{4}\bar{w}_{uk}c_{k}+\omega_{\mathrm{weak}}\min\{c_{2},c_{3},c_{4}\}. The benchmark utility for user type uu is Yu​(x,a)=wu​1​αfix​c1​(x,a)+(1−wu​1)​gu​(c2​(x,a),c3​(x,a),c4​(x,a))Y_{u}(x,a)=w_{u1}\,\alpha_{\mathrm{fix}}\,c_{1}(x,a)+(1-w_{u1})\,g_{u}\!\big(c_{2}(x,a),c_{3}(x,a),c_{4}(x,a)\big), and the evaluation target is the cached user-average surface qcache​(x,a)=𝔼⁡[YU​(x,a)∣X=x]q_{\mathrm{cache}}(x,a)=\mathbb{E}\!\left[Y_{U}(x,a)\mid X=x\right]. Representation-EXP maps each issue–patch pair into an auxiliary representation learned from observational patch statistics and fits EXP rewards on that representation. Appendix A.11 gives the public-data construction and the complete 5×55\times 5 results table.

With the data budget fixed, the ranking changes because the reward puts more or less weight on true fix success. The crossover occurs near αfix≈0.25\alpha_{\mathrm{fix}}\approx 0.25: below that point Representation-EXP is among the lowest-regret methods, and above it the best OBS-based methods overtake it. On the additive slice, the regret gap between Representation-EXP and the better of OBS-Only and CVCI moves from −0.0039-0.0039 at αfix=0\alpha_{\mathrm{fix}}=0 to +0.0003+0.0003 at αfix=0.25\alpha_{\mathrm{fix}}=0.25 and +0.0415+0.0415 at αfix=1\alpha_{\mathrm{fix}}=1. At ωweak=0.25\omega_{\mathrm{weak}}=0.25, the corresponding values are −0.0034-0.0034, +0.0024+0.0024, and +0.0375+0.0375. Figure 4 (left) shows the same crossover on the full 5×55\times 5 grid. This sweep tests whether the auxiliary patch statistics retain the target signal as the target moves from patch quality toward true fix success.

Held-out R2R^{2} comes from linear fits of the cached target using either the auxiliary patch statistics or c1c_{1} alone; Appendix A.11 gives the exact protocol. On the additive slice, the auxiliary-feature fit drops from R2=0.347R^{2}=0.347 at αfix=0\alpha_{\mathrm{fix}}=0 to 0.0810.081 at αfix=1\alpha_{\mathrm{fix}}=1, while the c1c_{1}-only fit rises from essentially zero to R2=0.967R^{2}=0.967. The R2R^{2} shift matches the change in method ranking: Representation-EXP helps when the target still follows patch-quality features, but it loses that advantage once the reward is driven mainly by fix success.

Changing ωweak\omega_{\mathrm{weak}} changes only how the non-success components are combined. Its largest effect is on Grounded: at zero fix-success weight, the grounded-minus-OBS regret gap shrinks from about +0.0495+0.0495 under additive scoring to about +0.0126+0.0126 under the pure weakest-link rule. Figure 4 (right) shows the same effect. Even so, Grounded remains worse than the best OBS-based method throughout this fixed-budget setting.

Benchmark-instantiation reading.

In this fixed-budget coding probe over the BouncerBench cached patch pool, Representation-EXP is the most competitive family in the regions where the auxiliary representation predicts the held-out cached target better than fix success alone (Figure 3, low-αfix\alpha_{\mathrm{fix}} cells). Once c1c_{1} alone predicts the target at least as well, the OBS-based families overtake Representation-EXP on held-out regret in the same probe (Figure 4). The pattern is a target-alignment diagnostic for this fixed-budget coding probe. Choosing among families in deployment would still require a live randomized trial.

6 Related work

The paper combines three literatures: off-policy evaluation, hybrid estimation from observational and randomized data, and LLM evaluation. Each covers only part of the setting. The setting combines confounded logging on real tasks, replayable text mediators that can be regenerated for any candidate model, and expensive outcome labels that are unbiased only inside a small randomized experiment.

Off-policy evaluation.

Direct Method with Replay (DM) and Doubly Robust (DR) are standard estimators in contextual-bandit and policy-evaluation settings (Dudík et al., 2011; Dudík et al., 2014; Swaminathan & Joachims, 2015; Jiang & Li, 2016; Thomas & Brunskill, 2016), and they descend from the foundational doubly robust and missing-data lineage of Robins et al. (1994) and Bang & Robins (2005). The OPE setting these papers analyze starts from logged action–outcome pairs in which outcomes are assumed unconfounded given context: the central technical issue is action coverage under the logging policy, and the recorded outcomes faithfully represent the causal target. In our setting, even for observed actions, the recorded outcomes are confounded because user-side factors influence both who selects which model and how its output is judged. Because SIM can regenerate outputs for any model on any held-out context, DM and DR enter only after the reward surface itself has been estimated. We use SIM and EXP to identify the causal scoring rule and then use OBS to reduce variance.

Experimental grounding and hybrid estimation.

The closest methodological antecedents are experimental grounding (Kallus et al., 2018), data-fusion and transportability formalisms (Pearl & Bareinboim, 2011; Bareinboim & Pearl, 2016), and trial-to-target generalizability (Cole & Stuart, 2010). A related line of work studies how to combine large biased samples with smaller randomized ones (Rosenman et al., 2023; Cheng & Cai, 2021; Lin et al., 2025; Yang et al., 2025; Colnet et al., 2024). That literature asks when observational signal can be used to reduce variance without giving up the causal credibility of the randomized sample; in those papers, the unit-level outcome is observed on both samples and the modeling work is done on a fixed outcome label. The estimator families in Section 4 are concrete instantiations of the same bias–variance question. Our setting differs in one specific way: the target outcome is not directly observed even on the randomized sample because the unit “output” must first be regenerated by SIM and then scored. Identification in our setting depends on SIM validity (Assumption A2) together with EXP randomization.

Summarization and LLM-based evaluation.

Our experiments use CNN/DailyMail contexts (Hermann et al., 2015; Nallapati et al., 2016; See et al., 2017; Stiennon et al., 2020) and rely on LLM-judged rubric scores in the pool-based study. Recent LLM-evaluation work covers benchmark design (Liang et al., 2023), judge reliability and pairwise preference platforms (Zheng et al., 2023; Chiang et al., 2024), and real-world usage logs (Zheng et al., 2024; Zhao et al., 2024). It also documents biases in automatic evaluators, including positional unfairness (Wang et al., 2023), length bias (Dubois et al., 2024), and self-preference (Panickssery et al., 2024), and studies panel-based mitigations (Verga et al., 2024). Preference data is central in alignment pipelines, both with explicit learned reward models (Christiano et al., 2017; Stiennon et al., 2020; Ouyang et al., 2022) and with implicit reward formulations such as direct preference optimization (Rafailov et al., 2023). The LLM-evaluation work cited above primarily treats judged scores as outcome data and studies how reliable those scores are and how to average them. We use cached outputs and judged scores as inputs to a causal evaluation problem; they become the causal target only after EXP-identified scoring.

A complementary line of work in causal NLP studies how text can serve as treatment, outcome, mediator, or proxy for unobserved confounders (Feder et al., 2022); OBS-derived auxiliary labels in our setting play exactly the proxy role identified there.

Taken together, the setting sits across the three literatures rather than fitting cleanly inside any one of them.

7 Discussion and Future Work

Ranking diagnostics can diverge sharply from recommendation regret. In the cached summarization benchmark, Grounded wins every top-1 and top-3 ranking setting but wins regret in only 6 settings. Regret is driven by a small number of costly recommendation mistakes that average ranking metrics do not isolate. The benchmarks therefore center Regrettest\mathrm{Regret}_{\mathrm{test}}, with context-action RMSE and model-level RMSE as secondary diagnostics.

What our cached benchmarks are and are not.

The two real-task benchmarks use real candidate model outputs and real LLM-judged rubric or program-test scores on those outputs. Their OBS and EXP mechanisms are benchmark constructions over the cached pool. The empirical comparisons therefore diagnose how the estimator families behave under controlled synthetic OBS/EXP resampling on real tasks.

Scope of the empirical benchmarks.

The empirical scope is deliberately narrow: cached summarization isolates supervision scarcity, and cached coding isolates reward geometry. Family-level wins in these benchmarks are benchmark-specific diagnostics.

Methodological implications.

Estimator choice depends on what limits performance in the benchmark at hand. In practice, the key checks are whether more EXP labels materially improve EXP-based methods and whether a structured representation predicts the held-out target better than a simple success-only baseline. Deployment decisions should still be confirmed by live randomized evaluation.

Limitations and future work.

These conclusions are specific to the task families and benchmark constructions studied here. Future work includes broader tasks, repeated mediator draws, naturally observed deployment logs paired with in-deployment randomized trials, and multi-round human–agent interaction, which would require relaxing or replacing Assumption A4.

8 Conclusion

Offline evaluation separates into identification and post-identification estimation. In the three-source design, the simulator and the randomized experiment together suffice to identify causal model values; the observational log helps only with estimation afterward, when its signal genuinely matches the causal target.

Across the controlled semi-synthetic validation and the two real-task cached benchmark constructions, different estimator families win in different regimes on held-out recommendation regret. The two benchmark families point to the same practical lesson: which estimator works best depends on both the amount of experimental supervision and on what the reward is actually trying to capture.

The results apply to one-shot cached-evaluation settings, not yet to richer interactive settings with repeated feedback and broader population-level uncertainty. Future work should extend the framework beyond one-shot cached evaluations to richer interactive settings and live deployment with randomized evaluation.

Appendix A Additional details

A.1 Identification remarks

SIM resolves generation; EXP resolves scoring.

SIM regenerates the mediator MM under do⁡(A=a)\mathrm{do}(A=a), while EXP supplies the outcome labels needed to score that mediator. So SIM handles counterfactual generation and EXP identifies causal scoring. The randomized sample is what identifies the scoring rule r⋆​(x,m)r^{\star}(x,m) for a realized context–output pair.

Why observational outcomes target a different object.

In deployment, AA depends on the latent variable UU, and UU also affects YY directly. Conditioning on (X,M)(X,M) therefore leaves self-selection bias in place, so in general

𝔼[Y∣X=x,M=m,OBS]≠r⋆(x,m).\mathbb{E}[Y\mid X=x,M=m,\mathrm{OBS}]\neq r^{\star}(x,m).

This is why the additional assumptions in Section 4 are estimator-side assumptions for using OBS, while identification itself comes from SIM and EXP.

A.2 Estimator details and concrete implementations

Exact reward-model objectives.

This subsection records the exact fitting problems and benchmark-specific implementation details deferred from Section 4. EXP-Only fits

(w^EXP,b^EXP)∈arg⁡min⁡∑j∈EXPw,b⁡(Yj−(w⊤​φ​(zj)+b))2+α​‖w‖22,(\widehat{w}_{\mathrm{EXP}},\widehat{b}_{\mathrm{EXP}})\in\arg\min_{w,b}\sum_{j\in\mathrm{EXP}}\big(Y_{j}-(w^{\top}\varphi(z_{j})+b)\big)^{2}+\alpha\|w\|_{2}^{2},

with prediction rule r^EXP​(z)=clip[0,1]​(w^EXP⊤​φ​(z)+b^EXP)\widehat{r}_{\mathrm{EXP}}(z)=\mathrm{clip}_{[0,1]}(\widehat{w}_{\mathrm{EXP}}^{\top}\varphi(z)+\widehat{b}_{\mathrm{EXP}}).

Representation-EXP fits the same ridge head on the proxy representation:

(w^ψ,b^ψ)∈arg⁡min⁡∑j∈EXPw,b⁡(Yj−(w⊤​ψ​(zj)+b))2+α​‖w‖22,(\widehat{w}_{\psi},\widehat{b}_{\psi})\in\arg\min_{w,b}\sum_{j\in\mathrm{EXP}}\big(Y_{j}-(w^{\top}\psi(z_{j})+b)\big)^{2}+\alpha\|w\|_{2}^{2},

with r^ψ​(z)=clip[0,1]​(w^ψ⊤​ψ​(z)+b^ψ)\widehat{r}_{\psi}(z)=\mathrm{clip}_{[0,1]}(\widehat{w}_{\psi}^{\top}\psi(z)+\widehat{b}_{\psi}).

OBS-Only fits the raw-feature ridge model on OBS outcomes,

(w^OBS,b^OBS)∈arg⁡min⁡∑i∈OBSw,b⁡(Yi−(w⊤​φ​(zi)+b))2+α​‖w‖22,(\widehat{w}_{\mathrm{OBS}},\widehat{b}_{\mathrm{OBS}})\in\arg\min_{w,b}\sum_{i\in\mathrm{OBS}}\big(Y_{i}-(w^{\top}\varphi(z_{i})+b)\big)^{2}+\alpha\|w\|_{2}^{2},

and predicts fOBS​(z)=clip[0,1]​(w^OBS⊤​φ​(z)+b^OBS)f_{\mathrm{OBS}}(z)=\mathrm{clip}_{[0,1]}(\widehat{w}_{\mathrm{OBS}}^{\top}\varphi(z)+\widehat{b}_{\mathrm{OBS}}).

For Grounded, define EXP residual targets Δj=fOBS​(zj)−Yj\Delta_{j}=f_{\mathrm{OBS}}(z_{j})-Y_{j} and fit

(θ^,c^)∈arg⁡min⁡∑j∈EXPθ,c⁡(Δj−(θ⊤​ψ​(zj)+c))2+λθ​‖θ‖22.(\widehat{\theta},\widehat{c})\in\arg\min_{\theta,c}\sum_{j\in\mathrm{EXP}}\big(\Delta_{j}-(\theta^{\top}\psi(z_{j})+c)\big)^{2}+\lambda_{\theta}\|\theta\|_{2}^{2}.

The resulting predictor subtracts the fitted proxy-side correction from the OBS baseline and clips the result to [0,1][0,1]. In the real benchmarks, the grounded family keeps the same outer form but replaces the single linear proxy correction with a small library of proxy-basis corrections built on the heuristic auxiliary proxy. Appendix A.3 compares this richer correction class with a single-linear baseline and with a weak pooled-anchor variant.

CVCI pools the OBS and EXP regression objectives:

CVCI-Residual residualizes around fOBSf_{\mathrm{OBS}} using the residual target Yj−fOBS​(zj)Y_{j}-f_{\mathrm{OBS}}(z_{j}) and pools only that residual fit in proxy space:

How each estimator family is implemented.

Table 8 shows how each estimator family is implemented in the appendix validation and in the two real benchmarks. The family names are the same across settings, but the proxy construction and EXP-side tuning differ by benchmark.

Throughout Section 5.3.1, Grounded refers to the rich proxy-basis version in Table 8. Appendix A.3 compares it with the single-linear baseline and the pooled-anchor variant.

A.3 Grounded-family implementations for the real cached benchmark

A common grounded template.

All real-benchmark grounded variants start from the same decomposition: fit an OBS baseline fOBSf_{\mathrm{OBS}} from logged outcomes, then use the heuristic auxiliary proxy to estimate a correction that is subtracted from that baseline. The variants differ along two design axes:

  1. 1.

    the correction class used on the proxy representation, and

  2. 2.

    whether OBS enters the second stage only through fOBSf_{\mathrm{OBS}} or also through a small pooled anchor after the correction direction has been fixed.

The grounded-family comparison instead organizes three principled instantiations of the same baseline-minus-correction idea.

Variant 1: single-linear grounded correction.

This is the most straightforward grounded instantiation. It uses the heuristic auxiliary proxy, keeps a single linear correction family, and tunes the correction strength on EXP. For the auxiliary real summarization comparison over β∈{0,0.2,0.5,0.8,0.9,0.99}\beta\in\{0,0.2,0.5,0.8,0.9,0.99\}, nOBS∈{2,000,20,000}n_{\mathrm{OBS}}\in\{2{,}000,20{,}000\}, and nEXP∈{20,100}n_{\mathrm{EXP}}\in\{20,100\}, we report the version of this linear class tuned by model-level EXP cross-validation, which serves as the matched linear baseline for the richer grounded variants. That single-linear class uses the predictor

r^lin,α​(z)=clip[0,1]​(fOBS​(z)−α⁡(θ^⊤​ψaux​(z)+c^)),\widehat{r}_{\mathrm{lin},\alpha}(z)=\mathrm{clip}_{[0,1]}\!\Big(f_{\mathrm{OBS}}(z)-\alpha\big(\widehat{\theta}^{\top}\psi_{\mathrm{aux}}(z)+\widehat{c}\big)\Big),

where ψaux\psi_{\mathrm{aux}} is the learned heuristic auxiliary proxy and the correction is linear in that proxy.

Variant 2: Grounded as a rich but still small proxy-side correction class.

The main-text Grounded instantiation keeps the same baseline-minus-correction outer form, but replaces the single linear correction by a small library of proxy-basis corrections. Write ψ~aux​(z)∈ℝ16\tilde{\psi}_{\mathrm{aux}}(z)\in\mathbb{R}^{16} for the standardized 16-dimensional SVD compression of the learned heuristic auxiliary proxy. For

B∈{Bid,Bpoly},Bid​(u)=u,Bpoly​(u)=[u,u⊙u],B\in\{B_{\mathrm{id}},B_{\mathrm{poly}}\},\qquad B_{\mathrm{id}}(u)=u,\qquad B_{\mathrm{poly}}(u)=\big[u,\ u\odot u\big],

and ridge level τ∈{10−2,1,100}\tau\in\{10^{-2},1,100\}, the rich grounded direction fits

(θ^B,τ,c^B,τ)∈arg⁡min⁡∑j∈EXPθ,c⁡(Δj−(θ⊤​B​(ψ~aux​(zj))+c))2+τ​‖θ‖22,Δj=fOBS​(zj)−Yj,(\widehat{\theta}_{B,\tau},\widehat{c}_{B,\tau})\in\arg\min_{\theta,c}\sum_{j\in\mathrm{EXP}}\big(\Delta_{j}-(\theta^{\top}B(\tilde{\psi}_{\mathrm{aux}}(z_{j}))+c)\big)^{2}\;+\;\tau\|\theta\|_{2}^{2},\qquad\Delta_{j}=f_{\mathrm{OBS}}(z_{j})-Y_{j},

and predicts

r^rich,B,α​(z)=clip[0,1]​(fOBS​(z)−α⁡(θ^B,τ⊤​B​(ψ~aux​(z))+c^B,τ)).\widehat{r}_{\mathrm{rich},B,\alpha}(z)=\mathrm{clip}_{[0,1]}\!\Big(f_{\mathrm{OBS}}(z)-\alpha\big(\widehat{\theta}_{B,\tau}^{\top}B(\tilde{\psi}_{\mathrm{aux}}(z))+\widehat{c}_{B,\tau}\big)\Big).

The final implementation selects (B,τ,α)(B,\tau,\alpha) by agent-CV on EXP. Relative to the linear grounded class, this replaces the correction family

ℋlin={u↦θ⊤u+c}\mathcal{H}_{\mathrm{lin}}=\Big\{u\mapsto\theta^{\top}u+c\Big\}

by

ℋrich={u↦θ⊤​B​(u)+c:B∈{Bid,Bpoly}},\mathcal{H}_{\mathrm{rich}}=\Big\{u\mapsto\theta^{\top}B(u)+c:\ B\in\{B_{\mathrm{id}},B_{\mathrm{poly}}\}\Big\},

so ℋlin⊆ℋrich\mathcal{H}_{\mathrm{lin}}\subseteq\mathcal{H}_{\mathrm{rich}}. The corresponding grounded predictor class therefore expands the proxy-side approximation space while still learning the correction direction from EXP only.

Variant 3: pooled-anchor grounded.

The appendix pooled-anchor variant keeps the rich EXP-only correction direction but adds a weak pooled anchor in the second stage. Let

c^B,τ​(z)=θ^B,τ⊤​B​(ψ~aux​(z))+c^B,τ\widehat{c}_{B,\tau}(z)=\widehat{\theta}_{B,\tau}^{\top}B(\tilde{\psi}_{\mathrm{aux}}(z))+\widehat{c}_{B,\tau}

denote the grounded correction direction learned from EXP. The pooled-anchor predictor is

r^anchor,λ​(z)=clip[0,1]​(b^λ​fOBS​(z)−α^λ​c^B,τ​(z)),\widehat{r}_{\mathrm{anchor},\lambda}(z)=\mathrm{clip}_{[0,1]}\!\Big(\widehat{b}_{\lambda}\,f_{\mathrm{OBS}}(z)-\widehat{\alpha}_{\lambda}\,\widehat{c}_{B,\tau}(z)\Big),

where (b^λ,α^λ)(\widehat{b}_{\lambda},\widehat{\alpha}_{\lambda}) are obtained from the anchored objective

(b^λ,α^λ)∈argminb,α[\displaystyle(\widehat{b}_{\lambda},\widehat{\alpha}_{\lambda})\in\arg\min_{b,\alpha}\Bigg[ λ​1nOBS​∑i∈OBS(Yi−(b​fOBScf​(zi)−α​c^B,τ​(zi)))2\displaystyle\lambda\,\frac{1}{n_{\mathrm{OBS}}}\sum_{i\in\mathrm{OBS}}\big(Y_{i}-(bf_{\mathrm{OBS}}^{\mathrm{cf}}(z_{i})-\alpha\widehat{c}_{B,\tau}(z_{i}))\big)^{2}
+(1−λ)1nEXP∑j∈EXP(Yj−(bfOBS(zj)−αc^B,τ(zj)))2]\displaystyle+(1-\lambda)\,\frac{1}{n_{\mathrm{EXP}}}\sum_{j\in\mathrm{EXP}}\big(Y_{j}-(bf_{\mathrm{OBS}}(z_{j})-\alpha\widehat{c}_{B,\tau}(z_{j}))\big)^{2}\Bigg]
+ρb​(b−1)2+ρα​(α−1)2.\displaystyle+\rho_{b}(b-1)^{2}+\rho_{\alpha}(\alpha-1)^{2}.

Here fOBScff_{\mathrm{OBS}}^{\mathrm{cf}} is a cross-fitted OBS baseline prediction. This variant pools only two calibration coefficients after EXP has already fixed the correction direction.

Why these implementations should behave differently.

The three variants place their modeling flexibility in different parts of the decomposition. The linear grounded baseline puts the entire second stage inside the smallest class ℋlin\mathcal{H}_{\mathrm{lin}}. So it is the most conservative option, but it can underfit whenever the discrepancy between fOBSf_{\mathrm{OBS}} and the causal target is only approximately linear in the proxy. Because Grounded replaces ℋlin\mathcal{H}_{\mathrm{lin}} by the strictly larger class ℋrich⊇ℋlin\mathcal{H}_{\mathrm{rich}}\supseteq\mathcal{H}_{\mathrm{lin}} while still estimating the correction direction from EXP only, it should help precisely when the residual mismatch is slightly nonlinear in the proxy yet still low-dimensional. The pooled-anchor variant changes a different part of the problem. It keeps the correction direction fixed at the grounded solution and lets OBS influence only the coarse scaling coefficients (b,α)(b,\alpha). It should help when the main issue is the relative calibration of the baseline and the correction, especially once EXP is large enough to identify a stable correction direction.

Results on the (β,nOBS,nEXP)(\beta,n_{\mathrm{OBS}},n_{\mathrm{EXP}}) comparison.

Relative to the matched single-linear baseline, Grounded lowers macro regret from 0.03570.0357 to 0.03180.0318, increases regret wins from 11 to 66, and has lower mean regret in 1515 of the 2424 (β,nOBS,nEXP)(\beta,n_{\mathrm{OBS}},n_{\mathrm{EXP}}) settings. The gains are concentrated in (2000,20)(2000,20) and (20000,100)(20000,100), where Grounded wins all six beta values, and in (20000,20)(20000,20), where it wins three of six.

The pooled-anchor variant behaves differently. It beats Grounded in 1111 of the 2424 settings and has the strongest average ranking metrics in this three-way comparison, but its macro regret is 0.03260.0326 and it wins regret in only four settings, all with nEXP=100n_{\mathrm{EXP}}=100. Those wins occur only when nEXP=100n_{\mathrm{EXP}}=100:

(β,nOBS,nEXP)∈{(0,2000,100),(0.5,2000,100),(0.8,20000,100),(0.9,20000,100)}.(\beta,n_{\mathrm{OBS}},n_{\mathrm{EXP}})\in\{(0,2000,100),\ (0.5,2000,100),\ (0.8,20000,100),\ (0.9,20000,100)\}.

The selected pooling weight is usually small: across 720720 fitted models, λ⋆≤0.03\lambda_{\star}\leq 0.03 in 565565 fits and λ⋆=0\lambda_{\star}=0 in 264264 fits. In this comparison, the pooled anchor changes calibration more than it changes the regret winner.

A.4 Value estimators and empirical benchmark metrics

The reward models in Section 4 estimate a conditional outcome surface. To obtain generative-model-level causal values, we combine those reward predictions with SIM. These DM / DR aggregators are used for the semi-synthetic generative-model values. They sit alongside the direct held-out-grid metrics in the real cached benchmark.

Let {xi}i=1neval\{x_{i}\}_{i=1}^{n_{\mathrm{eval}}} be evaluation contexts and let mi,a,b∼psim(⋅∣xi,a)m_{i,a,b}\sim p_{\mathrm{sim}}(\cdot\mid x_{i},a) denote SIM-generated mediators. The default SIM plug-in estimator is

μ^DM​(a)=1neval​∑i=1neval1B​∑b=1Br^​(xi,mi,a,b).\widehat{\mu}^{\mathrm{DM}}(a)=\frac{1}{n_{\mathrm{eval}}}\sum_{i=1}^{n_{\mathrm{eval}}}\frac{1}{B}\sum_{b=1}^{B}\widehat{r}(x_{i},m_{i,a,b}).

This simply averages predicted rewards over SIM-generated outputs.

A doubly robust variant augments the plug-in estimator with a residual term computed from EXP. Because EXP randomizes generative-model choice uniformly, pEXP​(a)=1/|𝒜EXP|p_{\mathrm{EXP}}(a)=1/|\mathcal{A}_{\mathrm{EXP}}|. Define

q^(x,a)=1BDR∑b=1BDRr^(x,ma,b),ma,b∼psim(⋅∣x,a),\widehat{q}(x,a)=\frac{1}{B_{\mathrm{DR}}}\sum_{b=1}^{B_{\mathrm{DR}}}\widehat{r}\big(x,m_{a,b}\big),\qquad m_{a,b}\sim p_{\mathrm{sim}}(\cdot\mid x,a),

as the Monte Carlo approximation to the SIM-integrated reward. The estimator is

μ^DR​(a)=1nEXP​∑j=1nEXPq^​(Xj,a)+1nEXP​∑j=1nEXP𝕀{Aj=a}pEXP​(a)​(Yj−r^​(Xj,Mj)).\widehat{\mu}^{\mathrm{DR}}(a)=\frac{1}{n_{\mathrm{EXP}}}\sum_{j=1}^{n_{\mathrm{EXP}}}\widehat{q}(X_{j},a)+\frac{1}{n_{\mathrm{EXP}}}\sum_{j=1}^{n_{\mathrm{EXP}}}\frac{\mathbb{I}\{A_{j}=a\}}{p_{\mathrm{EXP}}(a)}\big(Y_{j}-\widehat{r}(X_{j},M_{j})\big).

The first term is the SIM-based plug-in estimate. The second term corrects it using the randomized residual observed in EXP. For reward models trained on EXP, we use cross-fitting: EXP is partitioned into KcfK_{\mathrm{cf}} folds, and the reward model used in the residual term is trained on the remaining Kcf−1K_{\mathrm{cf}}-1 folds.

Role of DM / DR versus direct cached-benchmark metrics.

In the appendix semi-synthetic validation, we center held-out recommendation regret computed against the generator’s true interventional rewards. The same runs also produce model-level value diagnostics such as the agent-level RMSE of μ^DM​(a)\widehat{\mu}^{\mathrm{DM}}(a) or μ^DR​(a)\widehat{\mu}^{\mathrm{DR}}(a), which remain useful for diagnosing reward-surface fit. In the real cached benchmark, because the full held-out cached test grid is available, we additionally evaluate the fitted reward surface directly on that grid. Let 𝒳test\mathcal{X}_{\mathrm{test}} be the held-out test contexts and 𝒢test=𝒳test×𝒜\mathcal{G}_{\mathrm{test}}=\mathcal{X}_{\mathrm{test}}\times\mathcal{A} the held-out cached grid. For each (x,a)∈𝒢test(x,a)\in\mathcal{G}_{\mathrm{test}}, let qcache​(x,a)q_{\mathrm{cache}}(x,a) be the judged scalar reward of the single cached held-out trajectory for context xx and agent aa, and let q^​(x,a)\widehat{q}(x,a) be the fitted reward model evaluated on that cached trajectory. Define the benchmark-level agent aggregates

q¯cache​(a)=1|𝒳test|​∑x∈𝒳testqcache​(x,a),q¯pred​(a)=1|𝒳test|​∑x∈𝒳testq^​(x,a).\bar{q}_{\mathrm{cache}}(a)=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{X}_{\mathrm{test}}|}\sum_{x\in\mathcal{X}_{\mathrm{test}}}q_{\mathrm{cache}}(x,a),\qquad\bar{q}_{\mathrm{pred}}(a)=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{X}_{\mathrm{test}}|}\sum_{x\in\mathcal{X}_{\mathrm{test}}}\widehat{q}(x,a).

The real-benchmark empirical metrics are then

RMSEx​a=(1|𝒢test|​∑(x,a)∈𝒢test(q^​(x,a)−qcache​(x,a))2)1/2,\mathrm{RMSE}_{xa}=\left(\frac{1}{|\mathcal{G}_{\mathrm{test}}|}\sum_{(x,a)\in\mathcal{G}_{\mathrm{test}}}\big(\widehat{q}(x,a)-q_{\mathrm{cache}}(x,a)\big)^{2}\right)^{1/2},
RMSEagent=(1|𝒜|​∑a∈𝒜(q¯pred​(a)−q¯cache​(a))2)1/2,π^​(x)=arg⁡maxa∈𝒜​q^​(x,a),\mathrm{RMSE}_{\mathrm{agent}}=\left(\frac{1}{|\mathcal{A}|}\sum_{a\in\mathcal{A}}\big(\bar{q}_{\mathrm{pred}}(a)-\bar{q}_{\mathrm{cache}}(a)\big)^{2}\right)^{1/2},\qquad\widehat{\pi}(x)=\arg\max_{a\in\mathcal{A}}\widehat{q}(x,a),
Regrettest=1|𝒳test|​∑x∈𝒳test[maxa∈𝒜⁡qcache​(x,a)−qcache​(x,π^​(x))].\mathrm{Regret}_{\mathrm{test}}=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{X}_{\mathrm{test}}|}\sum_{x\in\mathcal{X}_{\mathrm{test}}}\Big[\max_{a\in\mathcal{A}}q_{\mathrm{cache}}(x,a)-q_{\mathrm{cache}}(x,\widehat{\pi}(x))\Big].

These real-benchmark metrics summarize the finite held-out cached grid. The natural next extension is repeated cached replays / repeated judged trajectories per (x,a)(x,a) so that the benchmark can estimate latent q⁡(x,a)q(x,a) more directly.
