Table 11 makes the heterogeneity explicit. OBS-Only improves in 2323 of the 3030 benchmark cells and becomes more favorable as nEXPn_{\mathrm{EXP}} grows. CVCI changes sign only at nEXP=800n_{\mathrm{EXP}}=800, where the residual term is large enough to help more than it hurts. The EXP-side methods behave differently: Representation-EXP worsens in 2828 of 3030 cells, and EXP-Only worsens in 2727 of 3030.

The natural interpretation is that DR is correcting the remaining OBS-side bias in model-level values rather than uniformly improving all fitted reward models. On this benchmark, that makes it most useful for the OBS-heavy baseline, conditionally useful for CVCI once the EXP budget is larger, and generally unhelpful for the EXP-side methods whose remaining error is not well summarized by a simple EXP residual correction.

A.7 Exact real benchmark protocol

Dataset and candidate generative models.

Contexts XX are CNN/DailyMail articles (Hermann et al., 2015; See et al., 2017). The candidate set contains 20 summarization systems: 16 prompt-based abstractive systems built from two Gemma 3 instruction models (Gemma Team, 2025), together with four extractive baselines. For each context–generative-model pair, the cache stores one summary together with its judged metadata.

Judged rewards and proxy features.

For each cached output, the judge returns rubric-style signals that are combined into the scalar reward used throughout the real benchmark comparisons. The real benchmark instead uses a heuristic auxiliary-feature channel derived from cached trajectories and judged-output metadata. That channel is best read as an OBS proxy, distinct from the hidden representation ϕ⋆\phi^{\star} used in the semi-synthetic study.

Fixed benchmark protocol.

The real-data study fixes a 48-context subset of relatively difficult CNN/DailyMail articles, selected once by an article-level difficulty score. Within this fixed pool, each seed performs an 80/2080/20 context-level train/test split, uses no separate context-level validation split, and tunes hyperparameters only on a held-out fraction of EXP when the estimator requires it. OBS and EXP are sampled only from the training contexts. The observational-choice protocol is a fixed paired-sampling design under a self-selection mechanism that routes each decision through a five-system candidate slate before the final model choice.

Budget views and aggregation.

The real summarization study uses three budget views. The main-text regret comparisons use

β∈{0,0.2,0.5,0.8,0.9,0.99},nOBS∈{2,000,20,000},nEXP∈{20,200},\beta\in\{0,0.2,0.5,0.8,0.9,0.99\},\qquad n_{\mathrm{OBS}}\in\{2{,}000,20{,}000\},\qquad n_{\mathrm{EXP}}\in\{20,200\},

with matched smooth and sharpened reward maps, giving the Section 5.3.1 summaries over six β\beta values, two OBS budgets, two EXP budgets, and two reward maps. The DM/DR value diagnostics in Table 11 instead fix nOBS=20,000n_{\mathrm{OBS}}=20{,}000 and use nEXP∈{100,200,800}n_{\mathrm{EXP}}\in\{100,200,800\}. The winner-map table below is a separate smooth-reward (β,nOBS,nEXP)(\beta,n_{\mathrm{OBS}},n_{\mathrm{EXP}}) comparison with

β∈{0,0.2,0.5,0.8,0.9,0.99},nOBS∈{2,000,20,000},nEXP∈{20,100},\beta\in\{0,0.2,0.5,0.8,0.9,0.99\},\qquad n_{\mathrm{OBS}}\in\{2{,}000,20{,}000\},\qquad n_{\mathrm{EXP}}\in\{20,100\},

reported to show the full 2424-cell winner map. All reported means and standard errors are recomputed from seed-level paired runs, with 30 seeds in every reported (β,nOBS,nEXP,method)(\beta,n_{\mathrm{OBS}},n_{\mathrm{EXP}},\text{method}) cell.

A.8 Tuning on EXP: model-level cross-validation, EXP holdout, and defaults

We use three EXP-side tuning strategies. Model-level EXP cross-validation partitions the generative models appearing in the sampled EXP data for that seed/cell and validates at the held-out model level over that sampled EXP model set. EXP holdout reserves a validation subset from the sampled nEXPn_{\mathrm{EXP}} budget itself and tunes on that holdout. Fixed defaults use dataset-configured settings with no extra EXP hyperparameter sweep.

More precisely, nEXPn_{\mathrm{EXP}} is the total EXP budget for a given seed/cell. If a method uses an explicit EXP holdout, that holdout is carved from the sampled EXP budget itself; no extra EXP rows are sampled outside budget, and no separate context-level validation split is required for this.

For Grounded-, CVCI-, and CVCI-Residual-style families tuned by model-level EXP cross-validation, let 𝒜EXP\mathcal{A}_{\mathrm{EXP}} be the set of generative models appearing in the sampled EXP data and partition it into KcvK_{\mathrm{cv}} folds {𝒜(k)}k=1Kcv\{\mathcal{A}^{(k)}\}_{k=1}^{K_{\mathrm{cv}}}. The corresponding validation indices are

ℐval(k)={j∈EXP:Aj∈𝒜(k)},ℐtr(k)=EXP∖ℐval(k).\mathcal{I}^{(k)}_{\mathrm{val}}=\{j\in\mathrm{EXP}:A_{j}\in\mathcal{A}^{(k)}\},\qquad\mathcal{I}^{(k)}_{\mathrm{tr}}=\mathrm{EXP}\setminus\mathcal{I}^{(k)}_{\mathrm{val}}.

For a candidate tuning parameter η\eta (for example, η=αcorr\eta=\alpha_{\mathrm{corr}} for Grounded or η=λ\eta=\lambda for CVCI), fit the corresponding estimator using all OBS data together with the EXP indices in ℐtr(k)\mathcal{I}^{(k)}_{\mathrm{tr}}. Then evaluate held-out generative-model means with

ℒ(k)​(η)=∑a∈𝒜(k)ωk,a​(r^¯η(k)​(a)−Y¯(k)​(a))2,\mathcal{L}^{(k)}(\eta)=\sum_{a\in\mathcal{A}^{(k)}}\omega_{k,a}\Big(\overline{\widehat{r}}_{\eta}^{(k)}(a)-\overline{Y}^{(k)}(a)\Big)^{2}, (7)

where r^¯η(k)(a)=1nk,a∑j∈ℐval(k):Aj=ar^η(−k)(zj)\overline{\widehat{r}}_{\eta}^{(k)}(a)=\tfrac{1}{n_{k,a}}\sum_{j\in\mathcal{I}^{(k)}_{\mathrm{val}}:\,A_{j}=a}\widehat{r}_{\eta}^{(-k)}(z_{j}), Y¯(k)(a)=1nk,a∑j∈ℐval(k):Aj=aYj\overline{Y}^{(k)}(a)=\tfrac{1}{n_{k,a}}\sum_{j\in\mathcal{I}^{(k)}_{\mathrm{val}}:\,A_{j}=a}Y_{j}, and nk,an_{k,a} is the number of held-out EXP examples for generative model aa in fold kk. We use count weights ωk,a∝nk,a\omega_{k,a}\propto n_{k,a}, normalized so that ∑a∈𝒜(k)ωk,a=1\sum_{a\in\mathcal{A}^{(k)}}\omega_{k,a}=1, and select the parameter that minimizes the average fold loss. If too few generative models appear in the sampled EXP data to sustain the requested number of model-level folds, the procedure falls back to sample-level cross-validation and records the effective mode.

In the real main sweep, Grounded, CVCI, and CVCI-Residual use model-level EXP cross-validation. The simpler historical linear grounded baseline instead uses an EXP holdout through correction-α\alpha tuning on the held-out EXP subset. EXP-Only, OBS-Only, and Representation-EXP use fixed defaults.

When candidate hyperparameters are tied within numerical tolerance, the implementation resolves ties toward the more regularized / less aggressive solution. For residual CVCI-Residual this means preferring larger residual ridge penalties and, if still tied, larger OBS pooling weights. For holdout-tuned grounded corrections, ties in the correction-α\alpha grid are resolved toward smaller shrinkage factors.

Because the news_hard top-48 real benchmark contains only 48 contexts, each 80/2080/20 context split leaves roughly 10 held-out test contexts per seed. Single-seed regret is therefore noisy, and all real-benchmark conclusions are aggregated across many seeds.

A.9 Semi-synthetic controlled validation

The semi-synthetic validation keeps the summarization task family but replaces judged rewards by a known latent generator, so held-out regret can be evaluated directly against the true interventional surface. Each context–mediator pair is mapped to an unobserved representation

ϕ⋆​(x,m)=H​φ​(x,m)∈ℝdϕ,\phi^{\star}(x,m)=H\varphi(x,m)\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{\phi}},

where HH is a fixed signed-hash projection of sparse hashed text features φ⁡(X,M)∈ℝ218\varphi(X,M)\in\mathbb{R}^{2^{18}}. The benchmark-specific outcome law is

PY(⋅∣x,m,u)=ℒ(sigmoid((w⋆)⊤ϕ⋆(x,m)+λ⊤u+ε)),ε∼𝒩(0,σY2),P_{Y}(\,\cdot\mid x,m,u)=\mathcal{L}\!\left(\operatorname{sigmoid}\!\big((w^{\star})^{\top}\phi^{\star}(x,m)+\lambda^{\top}u+\varepsilon\big)\right),\qquad\varepsilon\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\sigma_{Y}^{2}),

so

r⋆(x,m)=𝔼[Y∣X=x,M=m,EXP]=𝔼U∼P(⋅∣x),ε[sigmoid((w⋆)⊤ϕ⋆(x,m)+λ⊤U+ε)].r^{\star}(x,m)=\mathbb{E}[Y\mid X=x,M=m,\mathrm{EXP}]=\mathbb{E}_{U\sim P(\cdot\mid x),\,\varepsilon}\!\Big[\operatorname{sigmoid}\!\big((w^{\star})^{\top}\phi^{\star}(x,m)+\lambda^{\top}U+\varepsilon\big)\Big].

OBS and EXP share this same PYP_{Y}, so the only confounding channel is model choice through pOBSβ​(a∣x,u)p_{\mathrm{OBS}}^{\beta}(a\mid x,u), while EXP randomizes uniformly over the candidate agent set. This appendix validation varies only β\beta, nOBSn_{\mathrm{OBS}}, and nEXPn_{\mathrm{EXP}}, so changes in the regret winner can be attributed to confounding strength and data budget.

Implementation details.

The semi-synthetic generator uses sparse hashed text features φ⁡(X,M)∈ℝ218\varphi(X,M)\in\mathbb{R}^{2^{18}} for all reward models. The hidden representation has dimension dϕ=8d_{\phi}=8 and is constructed by a seeded signed-hash projection; it is fixed across replicates and is not observed by any estimator. When hybrid estimators use the proxy map ψ⁡(z)\psi(z) from Section 4, the PCA dimension is dψ=20d_{\psi}=20. The context-only embedding ψX​(X)\psi_{X}(X) that appears in the observational choice model is a separate object. It is fit on raw article text alone, with no context–output pairs. Operationally, we sample 5,000 contexts from the observational split, fit a TF–IDF vectorizer with English stop-word removal, unigram–bigram features, and a vocabulary cap of 50,000 terms, and then apply rank-50 truncated SVD. Thus ψX​(X)∈ℝ50\psi_{X}(X)\in\mathbb{R}^{50} is a low-dimensional context representation used only for model choice and for the U|XU\mid X model in the semi-synthetic generator. This is distinct from the proxy representation ψ⁡(X,M)\psi(X,M) in Section 4, which is learned from OBS auxiliary labels and is used by the hybrid reward estimators. Reference values and held-out regret metrics are computed on ntrue=100n_{\mathrm{true}}=100 and neval=100n_{\mathrm{eval}}=100 held-out contexts respectively, using B=5B=5 simulator draws per context–agent pair.

Fixed protocol in the appendix controlled validation.

The appendix semi-synthetic validation fixes one confounding protocol and varies only the self-selection weight β\beta, the observational budget nOBSn_{\mathrm{OBS}}, and the experimental budget nEXPn_{\mathrm{EXP}}. EXP randomizes uniformly over the candidate agent set. OBS mixes a context-only softmax policy with a latent-user shortlist policy, where β\beta is the probability of drawing from the confounded latent-user component. This validation uses

β∈{0,0.2,0.5,0.8,0.9,0.99},nOBS∈{2,000,20,000},nEXP∈{20,100},\beta\in\{0,0.2,0.5,0.8,0.9,0.99\},\qquad n_{\mathrm{OBS}}\in\{2{,}000,20{,}000\},\qquad n_{\mathrm{EXP}}\in\{20,100\},

and reports 30 paired seeds in every available cell. The direct latent effect on the reward score and the auxiliary-label noise level are both fixed throughout this validation grid.

Budget-axis repetition for pure baselines.

OBS-Only ignores EXP labels, so its reported value is constant across the two EXP columns for a fixed (β,nOBS)(\beta,n_{\mathrm{OBS}}) pair. EXP-Only ignores OBS outcomes, so its reported value is constant across the two OBS rows for a fixed (β,nEXP)(\beta,n_{\mathrm{EXP}}) pair. This repetition is carried through consistently in the synthetic regime table and summary table.

A.10 Appendix results for the summarization benchmark

Synthetic summarization results.

Table 12 shows the regret winner in each synthetic summarization setting over six β\beta values and four (nOBS,nEXP)(n_{\mathrm{OBS}},n_{\mathrm{EXP}}) budget settings.

The smallest-budget row (2,000,20)(2{,}000,20) is the most mixed: CVCI-Residual wins once, CVCI wins twice, OBS-Only wins once, and Grounded wins twice. At (20,000,20)(20{,}000,20), CVCI wins all six beta values. At (2,000,100)(2{,}000,100), the winner shifts from CVCI at lower β\beta to OBS-Only at higher β\beta. At (20,000,100)(20{,}000,100), EXP-Only wins all but the β=0\beta=0 cell.

Across the 24 settings, CVCI is the most stable overall winner, but no single method wins everywhere. Most regret gaps are small, so Table 12 is best read as a map of where the winner changes.

Additional synthetic aggregate interpretation.

Across the same 24 settings, CVCI is also the aggregate regret leader. EXP-Only and OBS-Only form the next tier, while Grounded and CVCI-Residual win only a few cells. The ranking diagnostics are flatter than regret: no single method leads top-1 or top-3 across the grid.

Real summarization results on the smooth auxiliary comparison.

Table 13 shows the regret winner in each real summarization setting for the auxiliary smooth-reward comparison over six β\beta values and four (nOBS,nEXP)(n_{\mathrm{OBS}},n_{\mathrm{EXP}}) budget settings.

At (2,000,20)(2{,}000,20), Grounded wins four beta values and OBS-Only wins two; the β=0.8\beta=0.8 cell is essentially a tie. At (20,000,20)(20{,}000,20), Grounded wins at low β\beta, while EXP-Only wins at higher β\beta. Once nEXP=100n_{\mathrm{EXP}}=100, the high-OBS row (20,000,100)(20{,}000,100) is dominated by CVCI, with a single CVCI-Residual win at β=0\beta=0, while the low-OBS row (2,000,100)(2{,}000,100) shifts from OBS-Only at lower β\beta to CVCI at higher β\beta.

Additional real ranking–regret comparison.

Across these 24 settings, CVCI is the aggregate regret leader and Grounded is second. Ranking tells a different story: Grounded wins top-1 and top-3 in all 24 settings but wins regret in only 6.

A.11 Public cached coding benchmark

Fixed protocol.

The coding benchmark uses a public cached grid of issue descriptions, patch mediators, and execution-derived rewards. The coding comparison in Section 5.3.1 fixes

β=0.5,nOBS=2,000,nEXP=100,\beta=0.5,\qquad n_{\mathrm{OBS}}=2{,}000,\qquad n_{\mathrm{EXP}}=100,

uses outcome-precision 6464, and evaluates only the feature-based implementations of the estimator families. It then varies two reward-design parameters:

fix-success weight∈{0,0.25,0.5,0.75,1},weakest-link weight∈{0,0.25,0.5,0.75,1},\text{fix-success weight}\in\{0,0.25,0.5,0.75,1\},\qquad\text{weakest-link weight}\in\{0,0.25,0.5,0.75,1\},

with 10 paired seeds in every cell. The first parameter rescales the fix-success component of the reward, while the second moves the non-fix patch-quality score from additive aggregation toward a weakest-link rule.

Appendix coding results.

In this coding appendix comparison, we treat a winner change as substantive when the top-two regret gap exceeds 3×10−33\times 10^{-3}; smaller gaps are near-ties. Table 14 reports the regret winner in each cell. Every top-two gap is below 0.010.01, and 2020 of the 2525 cells are below 1.5×10−31.5\times 10^{-3}. Most flips between OBS-Only and CVCI therefore reflect near-ties in the high-fix-success part of the grid. The clearest differences appear at low fix-success weight under additive scoring, where Representation-EXP outperforms the OBS-based methods, and in the steady narrowing of the grounded-versus-OBS gap as weakest-link scoring becomes stronger.

Secondary axes omitted from the main text.

Additional coding comparisons over confounding strength and outcome noise were qualitatively weaker. They changed absolute difficulty, but they did not produce ranking shifts as clear as those induced by the fix-success weight and weakest-link weight in this fixed-budget probe. For that reason, the main text centers this reward-design comparison and leaves the other axes to this appendix discussion.

A.12 Implementation notes

The synthetic validation uses only cached data generation; no external API calls occur after the generator pool is constructed. DR uses EXP propensities from uniform randomization together with cross-fitting for reward models trained on EXP. Additional synthetic diagnostics and older experimental variants are omitted from the present main-text comparisons.

Appendix B Rubric subscores for CNN/DailyMail summaries

Given an article XX and candidate summary MM, the judge outputs four integer subscores s~​(X,M)∈{0,1,2,3,4,5}4\tilde{s}(X,M)\in\{0,1,2,3,4,5\}^{4}: faithfulness, coverage, clarity, and conciseness. Scores use the anchors below; intermediate values interpolate between adjacent anchors.

Faithfulness (0–5).

Factual consistency with the article. Unsupported claims include invented entities, numbers, events, causal attributions, or quotes.

  • •

    5: No unsupported claims; all salient statements are grounded in XX.

  • •

    4: Minor unsupported detail(s) that do not affect the main facts.

  • •

    3: Multiple unsupported or weakly supported statements; main story remains recognizable.

  • •

    2: Several unsupported claims affecting key details (e.g., actor/action/outcome/number).

  • •

    1: Many unsupported claims; substantial contradiction or fabrication.

  • •

    0: Predominantly hallucinatory or contradictory relative to XX.

Coverage (0–5).

Inclusion of the article’s major points (headline facts, primary actors, core events, outcomes, and key qualifiers).

  • •

    5: Covers all major points; omissions are limited to minor details.

  • •

    4: Covers most major points; at most one major point missing.

  • •

    3: Covers some major points; several major omissions.

  • •

    2: Covers few major points; summary reflects only a small slice of the article.

  • •

    1: Minimal coverage; largely misses the article’s main content.

  • •

    0: Misses most major points or is largely off-topic relative to XX.

Clarity (0–5).

Readability and organization (coherence, grammaticality, referential clarity, and logical flow).

  • •

    5: Clear and well-structured; unambiguous references and fluent phrasing.

  • •

    4: Generally clear; minor awkwardness or minor ambiguity.

  • •

    3: Understandable with effort; noticeable disfluency, repetition, or unclear references.

  • •

    2: Hard to follow; frequent grammatical issues or unclear structure.

  • •

    1: Mostly unclear; major coherence failures.

  • •

    0: Unreadable or incoherent.

Conciseness (0–5).

Information density at an appropriate length; redundancy and irrelevant detail reduce the score; excessive brevity that omits necessary content also reduces the score.

  • •

    5: Efficient summary with minimal redundancy and no filler.

  • •

    4: Slight redundancy or mild over/under-length without major impact.

  • •

    3: Noticeable redundancy or length mismatch; still usable as a summary.

  • •

    2: Clearly too verbose or too terse; substantial inefficiency or truncation.

  • •

    1: Extremely verbose or extremely short; poor summary form.

  • •

    0: Pathological length or pervasive redundancy; not a usable summary.

Appendix C Full statements and proofs for identification and population estimator comparisons

This appendix collects the proof of the main identification result and the full statements and proofs for the population estimator comparisons referenced in Section 4. It also explains how these approximation-class results motivate the empirical target-alignment diagnostics used in the benchmarks; those diagnostics are not additional formal results. Throughout, Z=(X,M)Z=(X,M), PEP_{E} denotes the EXP law of ZZ, and for a fixed target outcome YY we write

ℛE​(f)=σE2+‖f−r⋆‖E2,‖g‖E2:=𝔼Z∼PE​[g​(Z)2],σE2:=𝔼⁡[(Y−r⋆​(Z))2∣EXP],\mathcal{R}_{E}(f)=\sigma_{E}^{2}+\|f-r^{\star}\|_{E}^{2},\qquad\|g\|_{E}^{2}:=\mathbb{E}_{Z\sim P_{E}}[g(Z)^{2}],\qquad\sigma_{E}^{2}:=\mathbb{E}\!\left[(Y-r^{\star}(Z))^{2}\mid\mathrm{EXP}\right], (8)

where r⋆(z):=𝔼[Y∣Z=z,EXP]r^{\star}(z):=\mathbb{E}[Y\mid Z=z,\mathrm{EXP}]. For readability, we ignore the final clipping to [0,1][0,1] and absorb the intercept into both ψ\psi and φ\varphi by augmenting them with a constant feature.

C.1 Proof of Theorem 1

Proof of Theorem 1.

This proves (1). Averaging q⁡(X,a)q(X,a) under the EXP context distribution and invoking Assumption A5 (PXtgt=PXEXPP_{X}^{\mathrm{tgt}}=P_{X}^{\mathrm{EXP}}) gives (2). Define the linear classes

ℋψ:={z↦θ⊤​ψ​(z):θ∈ℝdψ},ℱφ:={z↦w⊤​φ​(z):w∈ℝdφ},\mathcal{H}_{\psi}:=\{z\mapsto\theta^{\top}\psi(z):\theta\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{\psi}}\},\qquad\mathcal{F}_{\varphi}:=\{z\mapsto w^{\top}\varphi(z):w\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{\varphi}}\},

and the grounded / residual affine class

𝒢⁡(fOBS,ψ):={fOBS−h:h∈ℋψ}=fOBS+ℋψ,\mathcal{G}(f_{\mathrm{OBS}},\psi):=\{f_{\mathrm{OBS}}-h:\ h\in\mathcal{H}_{\psi}\}=f_{\mathrm{OBS}}+\mathcal{H}_{\psi},

where the equality uses that ℋψ\mathcal{H}_{\psi} is a linear space.

C.2 Summary of the fixed-target comparisons and empirical alignment diagnostics

The main text uses the population comparisons as conditional guidance for reading the experiments, not as a guarantee that one estimator dominates. We separate the formal results included below from empirical diagnostics that are motivated by the same approximation-gap viewpoint.

Formal results included below.
  • •

    At the oracle level, correcting OBS cannot hurt. Projecting OBS bias onto the correction space weakly improves EXP risk relative to OBS-Only; shrinkage matters only because the estimated correction can be noisy in finite samples. See Theorem 4.

  • •

    Grounded expands the proxy-side approximation class. If the OBS baseline is not already linear in ψ\psi, then correcting an expressive baseline by a low-dimensional proxy residual can represent targets that a pure ψ\psi-linear EXP fit cannot. See Theorem 2.

  • •

    CVCI-Residual is favored when the hard part is already in the OBS baseline. Residualization beats direct pooling when fOBSf_{\mathrm{OBS}} absorbs the difficult part of the reward surface and the remaining discrepancy is simpler in proxy space than the full target is in raw text features. See Theorem 3.

  • •

    In the shared linear proxy special case, Grounded is centered ridge. When both the OBS baseline and the EXP target are linear in the same proxy representation, Grounded becomes ridge centered at the OBS coefficient, and it beats EXP-Only exactly when that OBS center is a better shrinkage target than zero. See Theorem 5 and Corollary 6.

Empirical diagnostics motivated by the formal results.

The experiments do not test the oracle conditions directly. They report proxy-alignment and reward-shape diagnostics that are related to the approximation classes in the formal results. In summarization, the smooth-to-sharpened reward comparison changes the target while keeping the cached outputs fixed. In coding, the fix-success sweep moves the target away from auxiliary patch-quality features and toward true fix success. These diagnostics are empirical probes of estimator–target alignment, not additional theorems.

  • •

    Target–proxy alignment is measured empirically. The representation-based estimators are most useful when the target reward varies along directions retained by the auxiliary proxy. The summarization and coding experiments report held-out target-fit R2R^{2} as a proxy for this alignment.

  • •

    Reward definitions can change estimator rankings through approximation-class alignment. Changing the reward definition can move the target toward or away from the approximation class used by an estimator. The smooth/sharpened summarization comparison and the coding fix-success sweep are diagnostics consistent with this mechanism.

  • •

    Regret is the primary downstream metric. The experiments report recommendation regret because the evaluation objective is action selection; RMSE and ranking metrics are secondary diagnostics for reward-surface fit and model-level value fit.

C.3 What representation correction buys

Theorem 2 (What representation correction buys).

For any fixed baseline fOBSf_{\mathrm{OBS}}, the grounded class 𝒢⁡(fOBS,ψ)\mathcal{G}(f_{\mathrm{OBS}},\psi) satisfies the following three statements.

  1. (a)

    If there exists θ⋆∈ℝdψ\theta_{\star}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{\psi}} such that

    r⋆​(z)=fOBS​(z)−θ⋆⊤​ψ​(z)for all ​z,r^{\star}(z)=f_{\mathrm{OBS}}(z)-\theta_{\star}^{\top}\psi(z)\qquad\text{for all }z,

    then r⋆∈𝒢⁡(fOBS,ψ)r^{\star}\in\mathcal{G}(f_{\mathrm{OBS}},\psi). Conditional on the fitted baseline fOBSf_{\mathrm{OBS}}, EXP only needs to estimate the dψd_{\psi}-dimensional residual coefficient θ⋆\theta_{\star}.

  2. (b)

    If fOBS∉ℋψf_{\mathrm{OBS}}\notin\mathcal{H}_{\psi}, then

    𝒢⁡(fOBS,ψ)≠ℋψ,fOBS∈𝒢⁡(fOBS,ψ)∖ℋψ.\mathcal{G}(f_{\mathrm{OBS}},\psi)\neq\mathcal{H}_{\psi},\qquad f_{\mathrm{OBS}}\in\mathcal{G}(f_{\mathrm{OBS}},\psi)\setminus\mathcal{H}_{\psi}.

    So grounded correction can represent targets that a pure ψ\psi-linear EXP fit cannot.

  3. (c)

    If fOBS∈ℋψf_{\mathrm{OBS}}\in\mathcal{H}_{\psi}, then

    𝒢⁡(fOBS,ψ)=ℋψ.\mathcal{G}(f_{\mathrm{OBS}},\psi)=\mathcal{H}_{\psi}.

    In that special case, representation correction does not enlarge the function class.

Proof.

We prove the three claims in order.

For part (a), the displayed identity

r⋆​(z)=fOBS​(z)−θ⋆⊤​ψ​(z)r^{\star}(z)=f_{\mathrm{OBS}}(z)-\theta_{\star}^{\top}\psi(z)

is exactly the statement that r⋆∈𝒢⁡(fOBS,ψ)r^{\star}\in\mathcal{G}(f_{\mathrm{OBS}},\psi). Once fOBSf_{\mathrm{OBS}} is treated as fixed, the only EXP-side unknown is the dψd_{\psi}-dimensional coefficient vector θ⋆\theta_{\star}.

For part (b), note that 0∈ℋψ0\in\mathcal{H}_{\psi}, hence

fOBS=fOBS−0∈𝒢⁡(fOBS,ψ).f_{\mathrm{OBS}}=f_{\mathrm{OBS}}-0\in\mathcal{G}(f_{\mathrm{OBS}},\psi).

If 𝒢⁡(fOBS,ψ)=ℋψ\mathcal{G}(f_{\mathrm{OBS}},\psi)=\mathcal{H}_{\psi}, then this would imply fOBS∈ℋψf_{\mathrm{OBS}}\in\mathcal{H}_{\psi}, contradicting the assumption. Therefore 𝒢⁡(fOBS,ψ)≠ℋψ\mathcal{G}(f_{\mathrm{OBS}},\psi)\neq\mathcal{H}_{\psi}, and fOBSf_{\mathrm{OBS}} is a member of 𝒢⁡(fOBS,ψ)\mathcal{G}(f_{\mathrm{OBS}},\psi) that does not belong to ℋψ\mathcal{H}_{\psi}.

For part (c), suppose fOBS​(z)=βOBS⊤​ψ​(z)f_{\mathrm{OBS}}(z)=\beta_{\mathrm{OBS}}^{\top}\psi(z) for some βOBS∈ℝdψ\beta_{\mathrm{OBS}}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{\psi}}. Every g∈𝒢⁡(fOBS,ψ)g\in\mathcal{G}(f_{\mathrm{OBS}},\psi) has the form

g⁡(z)=βOBS⊤​ψ​(z)−θ⊤​ψ​(z)=(βOBS−θ)⊤​ψ​(z)∈ℋψ,g(z)=\beta_{\mathrm{OBS}}^{\top}\psi(z)-\theta^{\top}\psi(z)=(\beta_{\mathrm{OBS}}-\theta)^{\top}\psi(z)\in\mathcal{H}_{\psi},

so 𝒢⁡(fOBS,ψ)⊆ℋψ\mathcal{G}(f_{\mathrm{OBS}},\psi)\subseteq\mathcal{H}_{\psi}. Conversely, for any g⁡(z)=β⊤​ψ​(z)∈ℋψg(z)=\beta^{\top}\psi(z)\in\mathcal{H}_{\psi}, choosing θ=βOBS−β\theta=\beta_{\mathrm{OBS}}-\beta gives

g⁡(z)=fOBS​(z)−θ⊤​ψ​(z)∈𝒢⁡(fOBS,ψ).g(z)=f_{\mathrm{OBS}}(z)-\theta^{\top}\psi(z)\in\mathcal{G}(f_{\mathrm{OBS}},\psi).

Thus ℋψ⊆𝒢⁡(fOBS,ψ)\mathcal{H}_{\psi}\subseteq\mathcal{G}(f_{\mathrm{OBS}},\psi), proving equality. ∎

C.4 Residualization versus direct pooling

Theorem 3 (Residualization versus direct pooling).

Let fOBSf_{\mathrm{OBS}} be the observational baseline used by Grounded and CVCI-Residual, and assume fOBS,r⋆∈L2​(PE)f_{\mathrm{OBS}},r^{\star}\in L^{2}(P_{E}) together with finite-dimensional linear classes ℱφ\mathcal{F}_{\varphi} and ℋψ\mathcal{H}_{\psi}, so that both classes are closed in L2​(PE)L^{2}(P_{E}) and the projections in question exist (when arg⁡min\arg\min is non-unique, any minimizer suffices, since the displayed risks depend only on the projections). Define the oracle direct and residual predictors by

fcvci†∈arg⁡minf∈ℱφ​ℛE​(f),hres†∈arg⁡minh∈ℋψ​ℛE​(fOBS+h).f^{\dagger}_{\mathrm{cvci}}\in\arg\min_{f\in\mathcal{F}_{\varphi}}\mathcal{R}_{E}(f),\qquad h^{\dagger}_{\mathrm{res}}\in\arg\min_{h\in\mathcal{H}_{\psi}}\mathcal{R}_{E}(f_{\mathrm{OBS}}+h).

Then

ℛE​(fOBS+hres†)≤ℛE​(fcvci†)\mathcal{R}_{E}(f_{\mathrm{OBS}}+h^{\dagger}_{\mathrm{res}})\leq\mathcal{R}_{E}(f^{\dagger}_{\mathrm{cvci}})

if and only if

distE⁡(r⋆,fOBS+ℋψ)≤distE⁡(r⋆,ℱφ),\operatorname{dist}_{E}(r^{\star},f_{\mathrm{OBS}}+\mathcal{H}_{\psi})\leq\operatorname{dist}_{E}(r^{\star},\mathcal{F}_{\varphi}),

where distE⁡(r,𝒜):=infg∈𝒜‖r−g‖E\operatorname{dist}_{E}(r,\mathcal{A}):=\inf_{g\in\mathcal{A}}\|r-g\|_{E}. In particular, if

r⋆−fOBS∈ℋψbutr⋆∉ℱφ¯,r^{\star}-f_{\mathrm{OBS}}\in\mathcal{H}_{\psi}\qquad\text{but}\qquad r^{\star}\notin\overline{\mathcal{F}_{\varphi}},

then

ℛE​(fOBS+hres†)<ℛE​(fcvci†).\mathcal{R}_{E}(f_{\mathrm{OBS}}+h^{\dagger}_{\mathrm{res}})<\mathcal{R}_{E}(f^{\dagger}_{\mathrm{cvci}}).
Proof.

By (8),

inff∈ℱφℛE​(f)=σE2+inff∈ℱφ‖f−r⋆‖E2=σE2+distE2⁡(r⋆,ℱφ).\inf_{f\in\mathcal{F}_{\varphi}}\mathcal{R}_{E}(f)=\sigma_{E}^{2}+\inf_{f\in\mathcal{F}_{\varphi}}\|f-r^{\star}\|_{E}^{2}=\sigma_{E}^{2}+\operatorname{dist}_{E}^{2}(r^{\star},\mathcal{F}_{\varphi}).

Likewise,

infh∈ℋψℛE​(fOBS+h)=σE2+infh∈ℋψ‖fOBS+h−r⋆‖E2=σE2+distE2​(r⋆,fOBS+ℋψ).\inf_{h\in\mathcal{H}_{\psi}}\mathcal{R}_{E}(f_{\mathrm{OBS}}+h)=\sigma_{E}^{2}+\inf_{h\in\mathcal{H}_{\psi}}\|f_{\mathrm{OBS}}+h-r^{\star}\|_{E}^{2}=\sigma_{E}^{2}+\operatorname{dist}_{E}^{2}(r^{\star},f_{\mathrm{OBS}}+\mathcal{H}_{\psi}).

distE⁡(r⋆,fOBS+ℋψ)=0.\operatorname{dist}_{E}(r^{\star},f_{\mathrm{OBS}}+\mathcal{H}_{\psi})=0.

If also r⋆∉ℱφ¯r^{\star}\notin\overline{\mathcal{F}_{\varphi}}, then

distE⁡(r⋆,ℱφ)>0.\operatorname{dist}_{E}(r^{\star},\mathcal{F}_{\varphi})>0.

Hence

ℛE​(fOBS+hres†)<ℛE​(fcvci†).∎\mathcal{R}_{E}(f_{\mathrm{OBS}}+h^{\dagger}_{\mathrm{res}})<\mathcal{R}_{E}(f^{\dagger}_{\mathrm{cvci}}).\qed

C.5 Oracle grounding and shrinkage

Theorem 4 (Oracle grounding is no worse than OBS-only).

Let b:=fOBS−r⋆b:=f_{\mathrm{OBS}}-r^{\star} denote the OBS bias function on EXP. Let ℋψ⊂L2​(PE)\mathcal{H}_{\psi}\subset L^{2}(P_{E}) be the resulting closed linear correction space, and let

h†:=Πℋψ​bh^{\dagger}:=\Pi_{\mathcal{H}_{\psi}}b

be the L2​(PE)L^{2}(P_{E}) projection of bb onto that space. For any α∈[0,1]\alpha\in[0,1], define the oracle grounded predictor

fG,α:=fOBS−α​h†.f_{\mathrm{G},\alpha}:=f_{\mathrm{OBS}}-\alpha h^{\dagger}.

Then

ℛE​(fG,α)=ℛE​(fOBS)−(2​α−α2)​‖h†‖E2.\mathcal{R}_{E}(f_{\mathrm{G},\alpha})=\mathcal{R}_{E}(f_{\mathrm{OBS}})-(2\alpha-\alpha^{2})\|h^{\dagger}\|_{E}^{2}. (9)

Hence

ℛE​(fG,α)≤ℛE​(fOBS)for all ​α∈[0,1],\mathcal{R}_{E}(f_{\mathrm{G},\alpha})\leq\mathcal{R}_{E}(f_{\mathrm{OBS}})\qquad\text{for all }\alpha\in[0,1],

with strict inequality whenever α>0\alpha>0 and h†≠0h^{\dagger}\neq 0.

Proof.

Write

b=h†+u,u:=b−h†.b=h^{\dagger}+u,\qquad u:=b-h^{\dagger}.

Because h†h^{\dagger} is the orthogonal projection of bb onto the closed linear subspace ℋψ\mathcal{H}_{\psi}, we have u⟂h†u\perp h^{\dagger} in L2​(PE)L^{2}(P_{E}).

Now

fG,α−r⋆=(fOBS−r⋆)−α​h†=u+(1−α)​h†.f_{\mathrm{G},\alpha}-r^{\star}=(f_{\mathrm{OBS}}-r^{\star})-\alpha h^{\dagger}=u+(1-\alpha)h^{\dagger}.

Therefore,

ℛE​(fG,α)−σE2=‖u+(1−α)​h†‖E2=‖u‖E2+(1−α)2​‖h†‖E2,\mathcal{R}_{E}(f_{\mathrm{G},\alpha})-\sigma_{E}^{2}=\|u+(1-\alpha)h^{\dagger}\|_{E}^{2}=\|u\|_{E}^{2}+(1-\alpha)^{2}\|h^{\dagger}\|_{E}^{2},

where the cross term vanishes by orthogonality. On the other hand,

ℛE​(fOBS)−σE2=‖b‖E2=‖u+h†‖E2=‖u‖E2+‖h†‖E2.\mathcal{R}_{E}(f_{\mathrm{OBS}})-\sigma_{E}^{2}=\|b\|_{E}^{2}=\|u+h^{\dagger}\|_{E}^{2}=\|u\|_{E}^{2}+\|h^{\dagger}\|_{E}^{2}.

Subtracting the two displays gives

ℛE​(fG,α)−ℛE​(fOBS)=((1−α)2−1)​‖h†‖E2=−(2​α−α2)​‖h†‖E2,\mathcal{R}_{E}(f_{\mathrm{G},\alpha})-\mathcal{R}_{E}(f_{\mathrm{OBS}})=\bigl((1-\alpha)^{2}-1\bigr)\|h^{\dagger}\|_{E}^{2}=-(2\alpha-\alpha^{2})\|h^{\dagger}\|_{E}^{2},

which is (9). Since 2​α−α2≥02\alpha-\alpha^{2}\geq 0 on [0,1][0,1], the inequality follows, and it is strict whenever α>0\alpha>0 and h†≠0h^{\dagger}\neq 0. ∎

Derivation of the noisy-correction identity.

For any h~∈L2​(PE)\widetilde{h}\in L^{2}(P_{E}),

ℛE​(fOBS−α​h~)−ℛE​(fOBS)=α2​‖h~‖E2−2​α​⟨b,h~⟩E.\mathcal{R}_{E}(f_{\mathrm{OBS}}-\alpha\widetilde{h})-\mathcal{R}_{E}(f_{\mathrm{OBS}})=\alpha^{2}\|\widetilde{h}\|_{E}^{2}-2\alpha\langle b,\widetilde{h}\rangle_{E}. (10)

Indeed, fOBS−α​h~−r⋆=b−α​h~f_{\mathrm{OBS}}-\alpha\widetilde{h}-r^{\star}=b-\alpha\widetilde{h}, so

ℛE​(fOBS−α​h~)−σE2=‖b−α​h~‖E2=‖b‖E2+α2​‖h~‖E2−2​α​⟨b,h~⟩E.\mathcal{R}_{E}(f_{\mathrm{OBS}}-\alpha\widetilde{h})-\sigma_{E}^{2}=\|b-\alpha\widetilde{h}\|_{E}^{2}=\|b\|_{E}^{2}+\alpha^{2}\|\widetilde{h}\|_{E}^{2}-2\alpha\langle b,\widetilde{h}\rangle_{E}.

Subtracting ℛE​(fOBS)−σE2=‖b‖E2\mathcal{R}_{E}(f_{\mathrm{OBS}})-\sigma_{E}^{2}=\|b\|_{E}^{2} yields (10).

C.6 The shared linear proxy special case

Theorem 5 (Grounded is centered ridge in the linear proxy special case).

Assume the observational baseline is already linear in the proxy representation,

fOBS​(z)=βOBS⊤​ψ​(z),f_{\mathrm{OBS}}(z)=\beta_{\mathrm{OBS}}^{\top}\psi(z),

with the intercept absorbed into ψ\psi. Let the EXP sample be {(ψj,Yj)}j=1n\{(\psi_{j},Y_{j})\}_{j=1}^{n}, and write

Ψ=[ψ1⊤ψn⊤]∈ℝn×dψ,Y=(Y1,…,Yn)⊤.\Psi=\begin{bmatrix}\psi_{1}^{\top}\\ \vdots\\ \psi_{n}^{\top}\end{bmatrix}\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times d_{\psi}},\qquad Y=(Y_{1},\dots,Y_{n})^{\top}.

Under full correction αcorr=1\alpha_{\mathrm{corr}}=1, grounded correction solves

δ^∈arg⁡minδ∈ℝdψ⁡‖Ψ​βOBS−Y−Ψ​δ‖22+λ​‖δ‖22\widehat{\delta}\in\arg\min_{\delta\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{\psi}}}\|\Psi\beta_{\mathrm{OBS}}-Y-\Psi\delta\|_{2}^{2}+\lambda\|\delta\|_{2}^{2}

and outputs

β^G:=βOBS−δ^.\widehat{\beta}_{\mathrm{G}}:=\beta_{\mathrm{OBS}}-\widehat{\delta}.

Then β^G\widehat{\beta}_{\mathrm{G}} is exactly the centered ridge estimator

β^G∈arg⁡minβ∈ℝdψ⁡‖Y−Ψ​β‖22+λ​‖β−βOBS‖22.\widehat{\beta}_{\mathrm{G}}\in\arg\min_{\beta\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{\psi}}}\|Y-\Psi\beta\|_{2}^{2}+\lambda\|\beta-\beta_{\mathrm{OBS}}\|_{2}^{2}.

Equivalently,

β^G=(Ψ⊤​Ψ+λ​I)−1​(Ψ⊤​Y+λ​βOBS).\widehat{\beta}_{\mathrm{G}}=(\Psi^{\top}\Psi+\lambda I)^{-1}(\Psi^{\top}Y+\lambda\beta_{\mathrm{OBS}}).

For general αcorr∈[0,1]\alpha_{\mathrm{corr}}\in[0,1],

β^G,αcorr:=βOBS−αcorr​δ^=(1−αcorr)​βOBS+αcorr​β^G.\widehat{\beta}_{\mathrm{G},\alpha_{\mathrm{corr}}}:=\beta_{\mathrm{OBS}}-\alpha_{\mathrm{corr}}\widehat{\delta}=(1-\alpha_{\mathrm{corr}})\beta_{\mathrm{OBS}}+\alpha_{\mathrm{corr}}\widehat{\beta}_{\mathrm{G}}.
Proof.

Set

β=βOBS−δ.\beta=\beta_{\mathrm{OBS}}-\delta.

Then δ=βOBS−β\delta=\beta_{\mathrm{OBS}}-\beta, so

Ψ​βOBS−Y−Ψ​δ=Ψ​βOBS−Y−Ψ⁡(βOBS−β)=Ψ​β−Y.\Psi\beta_{\mathrm{OBS}}-Y-\Psi\delta=\Psi\beta_{\mathrm{OBS}}-Y-\Psi(\beta_{\mathrm{OBS}}-\beta)=\Psi\beta-Y.

Therefore

‖Ψ​βOBS−Y−Ψ​δ‖22+λ​‖δ‖22=‖Y−Ψ​β‖22+λ​‖β−βOBS‖22.\|\Psi\beta_{\mathrm{OBS}}-Y-\Psi\delta\|_{2}^{2}+\lambda\|\delta\|_{2}^{2}=\|Y-\Psi\beta\|_{2}^{2}+\lambda\|\beta-\beta_{\mathrm{OBS}}\|_{2}^{2}.

So minimizing over δ\delta is equivalent to minimizing over β\beta, which proves the centered-ridge representation.

For the closed form, differentiate the centered-ridge objective:

−2​Ψ⊤​(Y−Ψ​β)+2​λ​(β−βOBS)=0,-2\Psi^{\top}(Y-\Psi\beta)+2\lambda(\beta-\beta_{\mathrm{OBS}})=0,

hence

(Ψ⊤​Ψ+λ​I)​β=Ψ⊤​Y+λ​βOBS,(\Psi^{\top}\Psi+\lambda I)\beta=\Psi^{\top}Y+\lambda\beta_{\mathrm{OBS}},

which yields the stated formula for β^G\widehat{\beta}_{\mathrm{G}}.

Finally,

β^G,αcorr=βOBS−αcorr​δ^=βOBS−αcorr​(βOBS−β^G)=(1−αcorr)​βOBS+αcorr​β^G.∎\widehat{\beta}_{\mathrm{G},\alpha_{\mathrm{corr}}}=\beta_{\mathrm{OBS}}-\alpha_{\mathrm{corr}}\widehat{\delta}=\beta_{\mathrm{OBS}}-\alpha_{\mathrm{corr}}(\beta_{\mathrm{OBS}}-\widehat{\beta}_{\mathrm{G}})=(1-\alpha_{\mathrm{corr}})\beta_{\mathrm{OBS}}+\alpha_{\mathrm{corr}}\widehat{\beta}_{\mathrm{G}}.\qed
Corollary 6 (When the OBS center beats EXP-only).

Assume in addition that the EXP target is linear in the same representation,

Y=Ψ​β⋆+ε,𝔼⁡[ε∣Ψ]=0,Var⁡(ε∣Ψ)=σ2​In.Y=\Psi\beta_{\star}+\varepsilon,\qquad\mathbb{E}[\varepsilon\mid\Psi]=0,\qquad\operatorname{Var}(\varepsilon\mid\Psi)=\sigma^{2}I_{n}.

Let S:=Ψ⊤​ΨS:=\Psi^{\top}\Psi, A:=(S+λ​I)−1A:=(S+\lambda I)^{-1}, and define the EXP-only ridge estimator

β^EXP:=A​Ψ⊤​Y.\widehat{\beta}_{\mathrm{EXP}}:=A\Psi^{\top}Y.

For any positive semidefinite matrix GG, write ‖u‖G2:=u⊤​G​u\|u\|_{G}^{2}:=u^{\top}Gu. Then, conditional on Ψ\Psi,

𝔼⁡[‖β^G−β⋆‖G2∣Ψ]=λ2​(β⋆−βOBS)⊤​A​G​A​(β⋆−βOBS)+σ2​tr⁡(G​A​S​A),\mathbb{E}\!\left[\|\widehat{\beta}_{\mathrm{G}}-\beta_{\star}\|_{G}^{2}\mid\Psi\right]=\lambda^{2}(\beta_{\star}-\beta_{\mathrm{OBS}})^{\top}AGA(\beta_{\star}-\beta_{\mathrm{OBS}})+\sigma^{2}\operatorname{tr}(GASA),

while

𝔼⁡[‖β^EXP−β⋆‖G2∣Ψ]=λ2​β⋆⊤​A​G​A​β⋆+σ2​tr⁡(G​A​S​A).\mathbb{E}\!\left[\|\widehat{\beta}_{\mathrm{EXP}}-\beta_{\star}\|_{G}^{2}\mid\Psi\right]=\lambda^{2}\beta_{\star}^{\top}AGA\,\beta_{\star}+\sigma^{2}\operatorname{tr}(GASA).

Therefore the linear grounded estimator is better than EXP-Only if and only if

(β⋆−βOBS)⊤​A​G​A​(β⋆−βOBS)≤β⋆⊤​A​G​A​β⋆.(\beta_{\star}-\beta_{\mathrm{OBS}})^{\top}AGA(\beta_{\star}-\beta_{\mathrm{OBS}})\leq\beta_{\star}^{\top}AGA\,\beta_{\star}. (11)
Proof.

First,

β^EXP−β⋆=A​Ψ⊤​(Ψ​β⋆+ε)−β⋆=(A​S−I)​β⋆+A​Ψ⊤​ε.\widehat{\beta}_{\mathrm{EXP}}-\beta_{\star}=A\Psi^{\top}(\Psi\beta_{\star}+\varepsilon)-\beta_{\star}=(AS-I)\beta_{\star}+A\Psi^{\top}\varepsilon.

Since A​S−I=−λ​AAS-I=-\lambda A,

β^EXP−β⋆=−λ​A​β⋆+A​Ψ⊤​ε.\widehat{\beta}_{\mathrm{EXP}}-\beta_{\star}=-\lambda A\beta_{\star}+A\Psi^{\top}\varepsilon. (12)

For grounded, note that

Ψ​βOBS−Y=Ψ⁡(βOBS−β⋆)−ε=Ψ​δ⋆−ε.\Psi\beta_{\mathrm{OBS}}-Y=\Psi(\beta_{\mathrm{OBS}}-\beta_{\star})-\varepsilon=\Psi\delta_{\star}-\varepsilon.

Hence

β^G−β⋆=βOBS−β⋆−A​Ψ⊤​(Ψ​δ⋆−ε)=δ⋆−A​S​δ⋆+A​Ψ⊤​ε.\widehat{\beta}_{\mathrm{G}}-\beta_{\star}=\beta_{\mathrm{OBS}}-\beta_{\star}-A\Psi^{\top}(\Psi\delta_{\star}-\varepsilon)=\delta_{\star}-AS\delta_{\star}+A\Psi^{\top}\varepsilon.

Using I−A​S=λ​AI-AS=\lambda A gives

β^G−β⋆=λ​A​δ⋆+A​Ψ⊤​ε.\widehat{\beta}_{\mathrm{G}}-\beta_{\star}=\lambda A\delta_{\star}+A\Psi^{\top}\varepsilon. (13)

Now take conditional GG-risk. From (12),

𝔼⁡[‖β^EXP−β⋆‖G2∣Ψ]=λ2​β⋆⊤​A​G​A​β⋆+𝔼⁡[(A​Ψ⊤​ε)⊤​G​(A​Ψ⊤​ε)∣Ψ],\mathbb{E}\!\left[\|\widehat{\beta}_{\mathrm{EXP}}-\beta_{\star}\|_{G}^{2}\mid\Psi\right]=\lambda^{2}\beta_{\star}^{\top}AGA\,\beta_{\star}+\mathbb{E}\!\left[(A\Psi^{\top}\varepsilon)^{\top}G(A\Psi^{\top}\varepsilon)\mid\Psi\right],

because the cross term vanishes by 𝔼⁡[ε∣Ψ]=0\mathbb{E}[\varepsilon\mid\Psi]=0. The noise term is

𝔼⁡[(A​Ψ⊤​ε)⊤​G​(A​Ψ⊤​ε)∣Ψ]=tr⁡(G​A​Ψ⊤​𝔼​[ε​ε⊤∣Ψ]​Ψ​A)=σ2​tr⁡(G​A​S​A).\mathbb{E}\!\left[(A\Psi^{\top}\varepsilon)^{\top}G(A\Psi^{\top}\varepsilon)\mid\Psi\right]=\operatorname{tr}\!\left(GA\Psi^{\top}\,\mathbb{E}[\varepsilon\varepsilon^{\top}\mid\Psi]\,\Psi A\right)=\sigma^{2}\operatorname{tr}(GASA).

This gives the EXP-only expression.

The grounded formula is identical, replacing the bias vector −λ​A​β⋆-\lambda A\beta_{\star} by λ​A​δ⋆\lambda A\delta_{\star} from (13). Comparing the two expressions yields (11). ∎
